The payment represented wages paid in November and December, 1931, to employees of Canadian Pacific Railway shops, which the government arranged to have re-opened as an unemployment relief measure.

1012335,ca.proc.d.1934-02-05.18.1.1,1934-02-05,5f73217f-27d7-4bec-9943-554ca0daade8,ca.m.7834,Mr. A. A. HEAPS (North Winnipeg) moved:,,UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF,REDUCTION OF HOURS OF LABOUR AND INCREASE OF PURCHASING POWER,,Whereas, there still exists in Canada an acute unemployment problem, and
Whereas, it is desirable that as many as possible of these unemployed should be absorbed into the industrial life of the nation;

Therefore be it resolved, that, in the opinion of this house, the government should take into immediate consideration the necessity of reducing the hours of labour of those engaged in industry, and also increase the purchasing power of the masses of our people in order that they may absorb the goods produced, thereby creating a more equitable distribution of our wealth production.
He said:
column2: The motion I am submitting to

column1: the house to-day is very similar to one which I introduced a year ago and which was not accepted by the government. Immediately after the house prorogued, in June last I resubmitted this motion, and although it is about seven months since that I felt at the time that the problem of unemployment
would be just about as acute at the beginning of this session as it was at the previous session.

Those who have read the resolution will observe that it could be divided into three parts; one dealing with the question of purchasing power by the great masses of our people, the second dealing with the reduction of the hours of labour, and the third with the question of more equitable distribution of the wealth produced. To me, Mr. Speaker, probably the most important of the three parts is the one that deals with the increase of purchasing power of the masses of our people. In the increase of opportunities to consume more of the goods produced lies, in my opinion, the crux of the present economic situation. To me that is the only way we can begin to bring about a solution of the present unemployment situation. I feel that if we are going to settle the problem of unemployment there must be achieved a reasonable balance between production and consumption. At the present time production altogether outstrips consumption, and because of that unbalanced situation we have vast numbers of people in our dominion both on the farms and in the cities, who produce enormous quantities of commodities without having opportunity to consume the goods which they themselves produce. It has been suggested quite recently in this house, as well as in other places, that we ought to cut down on our production. I think that is the wrong way to set about arriving at a readjustment of our economic condition. I would far rather attempt to increase the consumptive opportunities of the people, instead of cutting down on their productivity. In- fact only a short time ago the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes), who I see in his place, was in Europe, and while discussing the wheat proposals of the various governments he suggested that instead of cutting down on wheat production they ought to attempt to increase the consumption in various parts of the world. I quite agreed with the sentiments then expressed by the minister, and I thought what an excellent thing it would be if he would in Canada preach here exactly the same thing he preached at the conference in London. The cutting down of our production is a form of industrial sabotage to which I am very much opposed. I feel that by cutting down production ultimately we are bound to have a reduced standard of living, and of course I am opposed to any reduction of our standard of living in Canada. I would far sooner see every effort advanced to bring about that increased consumption to which I have re-
Unemployment Relief-Mr. Heaps
ferred, and a little later I will attempt to explain what I mean by that statement.

To-day we have a huge surplus of commodities. Often this is termed over-production but I think properly it should be termed the surplus production which should have gone back into immediate consumptive channels, to those who directly and indirectly served in its production. We find a tremendous spread between the return to the labourer or the farmer and the prices paid for different commodities. I think in our industrial life it is taken for granted that even the best wages do not represent more than about one-third the cost of what the labourer produces, so two-thirds of the value of the commodities produced go, in profits of one form or another, to those who neither toil nor spin.

I ask for a reduction in the hours of labour, and why do I do that? It is not because men do not want to work; given the opportunity I think men are only too anxious to perform some useful function in our social life. I ask for a reduction in the hours of labour because to-day we have reached the stage in our technical progress and industrial advancement where it is not necessary for men and women to work the long hours that they are compelled to work at present. Just before coming to the chamber this afternoon I received a letter. from one of the large industrial centres of Quebec which stated that in a certain industry girls are working 69i hours per week for a wage of about $8. Men are working somewhat similar hours at high speed and with great efficiency, producing goods far in excess of what can be consumed either here or elsewhere. To-day there is no limit to our productive capacity; I think that is becoming generally recognized on all sides. If we have reached the stage in our technical progress when we can produce more than sufficient to satisfy all our requirements in a comparatively short time, then I think it may be said with a great deal of truth that the masses of the people have earned the right to greater leisure than they have enjoyed in the past.

In this dominion we have vast numbers of men and women who are out of work, as well as great numbers who are working on short time; in addition we have quite a number who are employed. I should like to put this proposition to the house: Supposing all the able-bodied men and women who are capable of performing a useful function in society were put into productive and useful employment; how long would it be necessary for that human energy, so harnessed to the machinery of production, to work in order to produce enough to satisfy all our human requirements? I venture to say that in the course of about 74726-16

twenty hours per week, on the average, there would be sufficient produced to satisfy all our needs and also allow for a reasonable surplus. There are men who have gone into this question rather carefully from a statistical point of view and they claim that with even less than twenty hours of work per week there could be sufficient produced, with the use of modern equipment, to satisfy all our requirements. Then, as I said before, if there has to be a reasonable balance between consumption and production, we have to see that the hours of labour are not in excess of what our consumptive needs really are. Therefore I say, Mr. Speaker, that if we are going to deal effectively with the unemployment situation in Canada it is essential that we reduce the hours of labour, because so far as I can see that is the only way we can ever hope to absorb into industry the vast numbers of men and women who to-day are out of work. Even if our industrial conditions in Canada continue to improve; even assuming that we return to the status of five or even ten years ago, of the half million or more men and women who are out of work to-day there will be hundreds and thousands who never again will be absorbed by the industrial life of this country. The other day the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) computed the number of people out of work as

column2: I do not know whether or not that is a correct estimate, but according to my information I should be inclined to think it an under-estimate if anything. It is quite true that there has been a slight improvement in the past few months, but it is impossible to say whether this improvement is of a permanent or temporary nature.

column1: Various remedies have been suggested to meet the situation. We have had the remedies brought in by the government during the past few years. We have had high tariffs* introduced as a means of increasing employment; we have had public works as another means of dealing with the situation, and then we have had the granting of relief to the hundreds of thousands, in fact millions, of our people who have found themselves in the unfortunate position of being compelled to seek assistance from public bodies. The fact is that to-day we realize perhaps more than we have ever realized before that the so called remedies which have been put into effect in the past few years have not been remedies for the situation at all, for if they had been remedies we would not be confronted to-day with half a million people unemployed in this dominion.
Unemployment Relief-Mr. Heaps

to a life of continual unemployment unless we do something radical to change the basis of our whole economic system. Many of these unemployed are simply drifting to-day, and among them can be heard the whispering of ideas which were never even entertained by them a few years ago.

We have heard hon. members of this house boast, and quite properly so, of the traditions of parliament, for after all parliament as we know it at the present time is the result of many long centuries of growth and development. It has taken practically seven hundred years of uninterrupted parliamentary government to bring us to the stage which we have reached to-day in the Dominion of Canada. In this democracy our ways of doing business are modelled after the pattern of Great Britain, and there parliamentary government goes back approximately seven hundred years, during which parliament has gone on uninterrupted in its course through all those centuries except for a brief period at the time of the revolution under Cromwell. Many people are, unfortunately, becoming tired of present institutions because when we come to deal from time to time with our fundamental problems such as unemployment, which affects the very basis of our economic life, appropriate and concrete action is not taken, or we pass the buck between the federal government and the provinces. I think the time has come when parliament should take a firm hold upon the situation and say that we are going to do something that will ameliorate the present conditions and give a ray of hope to those hundreds of thousands of men in this dominion who unfortunately find themselves idle with no prospect of work. I would dearly like to see our government do something radical to solve this particular problem. The fact that a motion of the government passed this house a few days ago to appoint a committee to make a far-reaching inquiry is an indication that at times the government is willing to make a radical departure from past precedent.

I would ask the government to look for a moment at what is happening south of the line. I am not one of those who can say at the moment whether what the people of the United States are doing is ultimately going to be a success or not, but we must give them credit for one thing, for making a tremendous effort to get out of those chaotic conditions in which they found themselves twelve months ago. But what are we doing here? We are simply going along in the same old rut, following the same old line as in past years, trusting, like Micawber, that something will turn up and bring about improvement in

conditions. We have been hoping and praying for such an improvement for four or five years, but no improvement in conditions that is worth mentioning has materialized; we still have those hundreds of thousands of men out of work with no hope of ever being able to be reabsorbed into the industrial life of this country.

As I said at the outset, if we are going to deal with this question of unemployment, of reabsorbing the hundreds of thousands of men and women who are out of work into our industrial life, there is only one thing we can do, and that is to provide them with work, and the way to provide them with permanent work is not by the creation of public works, desirable as that may be as a temporary palliative. No, Mr. Speaker, the only way in which you can find them work of a permanent character is by finding a way to reabsorb them into the industrial life of the country, where they will be producing goods that will get into the consumers' hands, and where the consumer will have an opportunity of consuming the goods which he has helped to produce. If they are going to be reabsorbed into the industrial life of this country, it is obvious that if we are going to work eight and ten and twelve hours a day as people are doing at the present time, we shall be able to produce far in excess of the consumptive capacities of the people. On the other hand, if we are going to absorb these people into the industrial life of the country so that all men and women may be properly absorbed and become useful citizens instead of considering themselves, as many of them do to-day, more or less useless citizens, consuming things which they have never helped to produce, it is necessary that the work should be limited to so many hours per day.

I ask the government to take this matter very seriously into their consideration. I realize how very difficult is the task ahead of any government that attempts to attack the unemployment problem in a fundamental way, and especially when it is attempted to be tackled under our present economic structure with any hope of even partially solving the problem. But as I have said before, from my seat in this house, it appears to me that the only way we can begin to solve this problem is, first of all, to put into the hands' of the great masses of our people a largely increased purchasing power as compared with what they have at the present time. Secondly we must reduce the hours of labour all around in order that the unemployed can be reabsorbed into our industrial life. We must give to the great masses of our people an opportunity of consuming the goods they produce. There must
Unemployment Relief-Mr. Maclnnis

be a more equitable distribution of the wealth that is produced. We cannot have that lopsided situation which exists in this country to-day, as in other countries, where we find a superabundance on the one hand and poverty on the other. That I think is recognized by all hon. members in the house as a situation which we here perhaps shall not tolerate much longer. All parties recognize the fact that a more equitable distribution of wealth is desirable, and it is coming to be recognized everywhere that there must be a reduction in the hours of labour. The members of this house, I believe, realize now that the labourer who is worthy of his hire is worthy of something more than he has received in the past. Therefore I would ask the government this afternoon to make some statement that will impart to our men and women, all those who find themselves out of work through no fault of their own, the hundreds of thousands who are unwillingly condemned to a life of idleness, some real hope so that in the not distant future they can look forward to being reabsorbed as useful citizens into the industrial life of the dominion.

,Labour,,Abraham Albert Heaps,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=5f73217f-27d7-4bec-9943-554ca0daade8&Language=E&Section=ALL
1012336,ca.proc.d.1934-02-05.18.1.2,1934-02-05,b8094e9f-95f3-46b2-ab3e-9e132f32ed9e,ca.m.8036,Mr. ANGUS MacINNIS (Vancouver South):,,UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF,REDUCTION OF HOURS OF LABOUR AND INCREASE OF PURCHASING POWER,,I think we are ajl agreed that the unemployment problem is the most serious question that faces not only this country but practically every other nation in the world to-day. It is not merely the fact that men and women are -unemployed and that they are suffering the misery and want which people in that condition necessarily suffer. The trouble is much deeper than that. There is something really more than the mere physical suffering to be considered; there is something more; the effect which this lowered standard of living will have on the future of the people of this dominion.

The social service council in the province of British Columbia held their annual meeting some little time ago and a very significant statement was made then by Miss Laura Holland, C.B.E., who by the way was one of the persons upon whom honours were conferred in the New Year's list. Apparently she was not troubled very much about whether she would receive an honour or not, but she was greatly troubled about the condition that, exists to-day in the ranks of the unemployed. She said that the greatest problem facing the country -at the present time was how to restore the destroyed morale of those who were affected through unemployment by this depression. This is the problem that is facing the Dominion of Canada to-day. If it were merely a matter of restoring tangible things,
they could be restored just as they were restored after the war in a very short time. But when, the spiritual and moral life of the people is destroyed it cannot be restored so quickly.

Now, no one can deny that deterioration in this direction has been taking place during the last four or five years. The committee on homeless men, at the same meeting, submitted a report in regard to these men. The homeless men are to a large extent young men who have reached the age of twenty-one and they are -then told by the relief department in Vancouver that thej' are no longer eligible for relief, so that they must go to the unemployment camps. But when they go to the unemployment camps they are met with the objection that they -are not homeless; their parents, they are told, are living in Vancouver and are responsible for their livelihood. But the fact is that in a large number of oases the parents themselves are on relief, so that the chairman of the committee, reporting on the matter, said that it had been amply proved that some of those young men had performed criminal acts in order that they might obtain the means of subsistence.

That is the condition that is facing the country at the present -time, and this resolution, I can assure the house, is not put forward as in itself a solution of the problem. Rather, it is put forward in the hope that it will receive some consideration, as one of the major questions involved in any plan that aims at the restoration of economic stability in this country.

I remember that when two years ago the hon. member for North Winnipeg introduced a similar resolution certain objections were brought forward against it. One objection was on the usual constitutional ground, that it was not within the constitutional powers of the dominion government to deal with the question of hours of work. That may be so, but to-day the government is finding itself in the position that, no matter how sacred we may consider the constitution, that constitution, as it is at present, no longer meets the situation. The government is therefore compelled daily to do things which at other times might be considered to be outside the jurisdiction of the dominion. So that in this regard the government has certain powers which it can bring to bear upon the provincial governments in order to make them act with respect to this matter of the reduction of hours. The other objection, as far as I remember, was raised by the hon. member for W'etaskiwin (Mr. Irvine), who pointed out that the reduction of hours and the increase
Unemployment Relief-Mr. Maclnnis

of wages was impossible under the profit system. I am willing to concede that point in the long run; indeed, I am willing to go further than that and to say that the profit system itself is impossible-and the impossibility of it has been conceded by almost everyone. It is because of that that in any general plan of reconstruction, not under the profit system but under a system of producing goods to meet the needs of the people, this question must be given due consideration. A few years ago, I take it, it would have been considered quite beyond the jurisdiction of the Dominion government to take any steps in regard to the reduction of wheat acreage, but that is being done to-day, and as a matter of fact the unemployment problem is approximately on all fours with the problem of wheat production. The only way by which the unemployment problem can be solved is through the provision of work for the unemployed.

Now, the only way to provide a solution for the difficulties that confront the wheat farmers is to ensure a market for their wheat; but if you cannot ensure a market for their wheat to the extent of its production, then the idea is to restrict the supply in order to meet the demand. Well, the same applies to the labour movement. If there are not enough jobs for, let us say, one million workers at eight hours a day, then the logical solution is not to put five hundred thousand to work at eight hours a day, placing the other five hundred thousand unemployed on relief, but to put the one million workers to work at four hours a day. There is another logical reason for this. We talk about the expense of unemployment but regardless of expense, the unemployed are fed, clothed and sheltered by those who are working. It is the men who are working to produce food, clothing and shelter upon whom the burden falls ultimately, and not on those who may be called upon to supply the money tokens by which relief is financed. So that from that point of view I think it would be far more fair to put the unemployed to work and thus ease the burden of work on those who are already employed.

The first year I was here, the first regular session in 1931, I pointed out that one of the root causes of unemployment, that is, outside the general capitalistic system itself, was that the producers do not receive enough in purchasing power to enable them to consume the products of their labour, while the owning class, those who receive their rewards in rent, interest and profit, are unable to consume the remainder of the goods thus produced. But

It is not contended that if wages were slightly higher there would not be any unemployment, but it is contended that if less were going into dividends and more into wages which would be used altogether in the purchase of consumers' goods, the depression could have been eased considerably. So far as I know we have not general figures for the dominion, but we have them for the United States and conditions there are similar to those here. All we need do in most cases is to reduce them according to population and we have a picture of conditions as they prevail in this country. These figures are compiled by the Federal Bureau of Foreign and Domestic Commerce of the United States in cooperation with the National Bureau of Economic Research and are for the period from 1929 to

1932. The total income distributed to individuals in 1929 was $81,000,000,000. In 1930 it dropped to $75,000,000,000, in 1931 to $63,000,000,000, and in 1932 to $49,000,000,000. In 1929 the actual earned income was

1012341,ca.proc.d.1934-02-05.18.1.7,1934-02-05,48fe0415-1454-43d8-a242-1562dedacc97,ca.m.2450,Mr. HUMPHREY MITCHELL (East Hamilton):,,UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF,REDUCTION OF HOURS OF LABOUR AND INCREASE OF PURCHASING POWER,,Before the debate concludes,

Mr. Speaker, I should like to make just one or two observations on the resolution now before the house. I should like to tell the government that this resolution is in keeping with the time-honoured policy of the trade union movement in this country, which for many years has advocated, and insisted upon with some success, a reduction in the hours of labour, with no reduction in the consuming power of the workers. To me it is almost marvellous to see the crystallization of world opinion as to the soundness of the position taken by the official trade union movement as to hours of labour in industry. Had it not been for the very necessary educational program carried on by the American Federation of Labor I believe it will be agreed that the experiment embodied in the N.R.A. would not have been possible in the great republic to the south. Notwithstanding what views we may hold as to that experiment, in my opinion it is the greatest experiment in the history of democratic nations up to this time. After all is said and done it took some courage to make the decision that was made by the president of the United States, which launched this far-reaching campaign in an effort to adjust the output of industry and agriculture to the consuming power of the people of the United States.

I believe the world at large looks upon this experiment with a great deal of sympathy, in the hope that it may prove successful and give leadership to the rest of the civilized world. I was in London during the economic conference this year, a conference that was stillborn because the leaders of national thought in the various countries there represented had not the vision and the courage to appreciate the possibilities of the American experiment. I believe that had there been a world approach to the problem of unemployment and mass production in agriculture and industry, rather than a national approach on the part of the American government an entirely different condition would to-day exist in the world. Of course, the story of what happened at the economic conference was so simple and obvious that it is scarcely worth retelling. I mean simply this, that the gold bloc went there with the definite intention of destroying the usefulness of the conference, the British delegates sat on the fence and the Americans fell out among themselves.

Since the beginning of the session there have been a number of speeches. I should like to feel that the representatives of the people would spend as much time, effort and energy on an important problem such as that which is now before us as they would in a discussion on titles, a resurrection of the old cannibal days when men wore beads around their necks and rings in their noses. I would rather see hon. members concentrate on the real problems confronting our men and women. Even in the boom days of 1928 we were confronted with the same problem. We are apt to forget those days; we are apt to forget the difficulty with which we will be confronted if we ever emerge from this depression-I mean that of being too old at forty-five. That is the real tragedy in the life of this young and growing industrial nation. That is one of the aspects of the resolution presented by the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps). I believe it is fair to state that our progress is held in check by our inability to consume the products of the fields and the factories. The statement is often made to the industrial worker that his one aim should be that of increasing his leisure hours. That is not the correct view. The argument for shorter hours rests upon the practical foundation of our ability to consume in super-abundance. If this question of production and consumption is not dealt with it has the possibility of destroying the veiy civilization we have erected. In my view this problem is so simple that the arguments of those discussing it cannot be controverted. I believe it is fair to ask this House of Commons, reflecting as it does the aims and desires of the Canadian people, what it is going to do about it.
I believe it is fair to say that the industrial technique and makeup of Canada is somewhat similar to that of the United States. Between the years 1919 and 1933 in that

column2: COMMONS

column1: Unemployment Relief-Mr. Mitchell

country the productive capacity of the individual increased by 83 per cent. Between the years 1926 and 1933 it increased by 30 per cent. The remedy for the change is obvious and must, I believe, follow the suggestions contained in the resolution now before us. I remember that in my first session in the house, only two short years ago, I asked a simple question of the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) with reference to the activities of our delegates at a meeting of the international labour office, held in Washington in the year 1919. He made light of my observations concerning the necessity for a reduction of the hours of labour. He said, ""Some day you will want a six-hour working day."" I said, ""Yes, I will live to see the day when there will be a four-hour working day in Canada."" In those two short years we have seen the government of the United States, under the policy of the N.R.A. insisting upon a six-hour day in connection with certain industries and undertakings. That, Mr. Speaker, goes to show the soundness of the vision and the position taken by the men and women who go to make up the trade union movement in Canada. The problem of hours of labour is one in connection with which the government could take a lead. I believe it is fair to say that our industrial and financial leaders have forgotten that they ever led; I question very much whether or not they ever did lead. I believe they were just carried along on a tide of enthusiasm. Had the government adopted the resolution submitted last session by the hon. member for North Winnipeg there would have been no necessity for the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) to speak as he did in the city of Toronto. Had the resolution been adopted the information would have been secured last year instead of this year. The resolution of last session would have brought out all the facts, and we would have approached the problem having in mind the points of view of the men and women engaged in various walks of life.

I sometimes wonder at our helplessness. We cannot say that science or nature has failed us. Our only difficulty is lack of common sense, and our inability to comprehend the real menace confronting us. Although matters of labour have been of international importance, unfortunately our dominion from a . governmental and official standpoint has probably been more backward than any country in the civilized world. Only last year the Italian delegation to the League of Nations introduced a resolution backed by the government of that country calling for the immediate introduction of a forty-hour week into the industry of the nations connected

with the labour organization of the league. While it is quite true that no decision was made, we must admit that at least one government in the world has from its own experience realized the soundness of the position which for many years has been taken by Canadian labour.

Of course, there is not much use reducing the hours of labour if at the same time we do not increase consuming power. I believe that much of our difficulty has been brought about by the avarice of the investor and of the business men and financiers of this country. Unless you give the individual engaged in industry sufficient wages to buy back what he produces, inevitably you are facing trouble. You must make it possible for him and her to receive some measure of the fruits of technological progress. This is not a dream, it is not a theory; it is a positive fact predicated upon our past experience.

Those who believed that stacks of paper in 1928 were real wealth were just kidding themselves, and of course the inevitable windstorm came along and blew them out into the street. It would have been far better if they had given that money to the men and women engaged in industry with which to buy back the goods they produced, and thus keep the machine at least in some semblance of normal running order. I believe that that declaration is a . fundamental around which all society revolves, and until we are willing to meet that in a practical and realistic way this depression will not show any signs of lifting. What was the greatest tragedy of the machine era? Let me say that we are at the end of an era, whether we like it or not, and those people who think that the issue is between free trade and protection are just having a pipe dream, in my judgment. In the industrial era we concentrated on the machine to the exclusion of the human element in industry. We thought that so long as we produced and produced and produced, that was the solution of the problem, and we completely forgot the human being who, in the final analysis, is the basis of all civilization and life itself.

As an apprentice boy I have seen the development of the machine. I have seen men and women displaced overnight by an advancement in the technique of industry. Let me give you an illustration to show the extent to which the thing is drifting. Once upon a time we thought that all musicians were artists; in fadt, they thought so themselves. They thought that the machine would never affect their daily lives, that they were a class apart from men engaged in the
Unemployment Relief-Mr. Hanbury

normal industries of this country. Then the "" talkie "" was developed, and overnight it wiped out the means of livelihood of forty thousand musicians on the North American continent. Going even a step further, the mechanical hare was developed, to be chased by the whippets on the racecourse.

When I was crossing the Atlantic this year there was a Russian violinist on board, and I made this observation. I said it was passing strange that we from the great centres of civilization had to come out into the middle of the Atlantic to see one of the great artists play in the flesh. At home we got it through the medium of the machine. I went on to say that all we need to-day to complete the circle is to bring babies into the world in cans like tomatoes, and then of course there will be no use living at all.

I believe, Mr. Speaker, that the government, in carrying out its building program announced in the speech from the throne, should set an example in fixing the hours of labour on such works at such a level that the employment possibilities under that plan would be greatly increased, and at the same time it would be setting an example to employers throughout the dominion.

Mention has been made of the necessity of amending the British North America Act in order to set in motion any machinery for carrying out the object of this resolution. I am glad to record, Mr. Speaker, that opinion in this country is crystallizing in support of the view that has been expressed from this corner of the house for many years in regard to the British North America Act. Only the other day the premier of Ontario expressed the opinion that the British North America Act was in need of revision to bring it up to the standard of modern requirements in a country so vast as Canada.

I know what the argument of the government is going to be in reply to this resolution. They are going to say that nothing can be done unless all governments in all countries of the world do the same thing. I do not believe that we can wait for that. I do not believe that it is practical to wait for that. I believe that leadership should be given by the government of the day in exploring every channel whereby the driving force of this resolution might become a practical reality, instead of the resolution simply being allowed to be another resolution of this House of Commons. I should like to leave that thought with the government in connection with this resolution. I believe that it is as pressing, if indeed not more so, as any resolution that appears on the order paper from private members of this

house, as viewed from the standpoint of the industrial workers of this dominion, and I would urge the government to lend its aid in meeting this very practical problem confronting the industrial workers from one end of this broad dominion to the other.

Further on, the resolution-refers to increasing the purchasing power of "" the masses."" I really do not know whom the mover is referring to in his use of the words ""the masses."" I for one would like to have my purchasing power increased. Whether I am to be included in "" the masses "" I do not know. I think it is important that the purchasing power of all people in Canada should be increased. In the last line of the resolution he also refers to the equitable distribution of our wealth. I think it is important that we should have distribution, whether it is equitable or not. Of course, we should all like it to be equitable; but our problem to-day is that our production is not being consumed. If it were being consumed,
Unemployment Reliej-Mr. Fajard
whether equitably or not, there would be work for those at present unemployed.

The problem referred to by the previous speaker-and I wish to congratulate him on his remarks-was that of jurisdiction. At the present time jurisdiction in the regulation of hours of labour is a purely provincial matter. In the province of British Columbia from which I come, we have had what is commonly called advanced labour legislation, with regard to the regulation of hours of work and of rates of pay. We find in that province that, with higher rates of pay and shorter hours, and with many benefits to the workers for which industry must pay we are expected to compete with provinces in Canada where there are not such regulations. It must, however, be apparent to all the members of this house that such provincial regulation is really a restriction of industry. It is not only unfair to industry itself, but by virtue of the fact that it must eventually react against the worker, it is unfair to the worker in that province to that extent.

Then we come to the question of international trade. In the lumber industry of British Columbia, assume that we are obliged as a province to pay higher wages and further to regulate the hours of labour. Now, we are attempting to do, and are doing our lumber business throughout the markets of the world, but we are faced with competition with other nations where there are not in force the same regulations, and we are faced with some competition from those provinces of Canada in which similar regulations are not to be found.

These are problems which, as the previous speaker has said, must be met. We cannot continue as we are going at the present time and maintain the same degree of democracy and freedom if we do not come to some conclusion-not just consideration, but some conclusion-and at an early date, which will bring about a re-employment of those at present unemployed.

This of course raises a very great question, particularly in its international aspect. So far as I am personally concerned, and I think I can speak for many engaged in industry in British Columbia, we are quite prepared that the government should make some regulation that might have an adverse effect on our international trade, temporarily at least. We recognize that it would be a temporarily bad influence, but I think I can say that we also recognize that the national existence of Canada is probably more important at this stage than international trade. Therefore I wish heartily to support the resolution which is on
the order paper, and I would go further and suggest that instead of consideration something should be done and done at once.

In this connection, the first practical suggestion is that the provinces of Canada should gather with the federal authority and that we should have a realignment of authority in Canada. The regulation of hours of labour, rates of pay, conditions of lalbour-these do not constitute the only problem that faces the people to-day; nor is this problem the only one that requires that the Act of Confederation should be reconsidered and revamped. That is the first practical step, and until it is taken I do not see how we can make progress. We shall be receiving evasions and suggestions and criticisms for all time until that step is taken, and I therefore submit in all sincerity to the government that they should do what they can ito bring all the provinces of Canada into a conference that will redefine our confederation.

1012345,ca.proc.d.1934-02-05.18.1.11,1934-02-05,a63343dc-e727-4871-b2c0-a429c5621416,ca.m.8950,Mr. J. FERNAND FAFARD (L'lslet) (Translation):,,UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF,REDUCTION OF HOURS OF LABOUR AND INCREASE OF PURCHASING POWER,,Mr. Speaker, the resolution,

at present under consideration by the house requests that the hours of labour be reduced, and, at the same time, wages be increased. I did not think that this resolution would be discussed to-day. After closely following the speeches which have just been made, I deem it timely to make a few brief remarks.

If you increase the wages and reduce the working hours, it is evident that the manufactured products will cost far more and, therefore, our commerce will immediately suffer from it. I wonder if it is fair to request the farmer to work fifteen hours daily to sustain the workman who would only have to work six hours per day? It is said that the farmer is not obliged to work such long hours; however, any one who has lived among them, who has been brought up on the farm, knows fully well that the farmer must rise with the sun, that he must toil many hours, has no control over the working hours, nature sees to that; for instance, the morning dew is uncontrollable.
I wonder really whether it is fair to expect the farming class to work five or six times longer than the workmen, the consumers, and for less wages.
It was stated a few moments ago that the cause of the whole evil was not the tariff, but the various mechanical contrivances invented in the course of the last half century.
I cannot admit such an assertion. The real cause of the invention of machinery lies in the labour unrest which broke out everywhere. The workman always seemed discon-
Unemployment Relief-Mr. Stitt (Selkirk)

tented with his lot, and man's genius applied itself to overcome the difficulties encountered, by inventing machinery to supplement man's labour. Moreover, I do not think that mechanical contrivances are actually responsible for the depression the workman suffers. Take, for instance, printing; years ago, no country hardly published any books, because it necessitated too much labour and, therefore, was too costly. To-day, there are millions of men employed in the printing of newspapers and reviews of all kinds. And if one studies the subject more closely, he will find that these mechanical devices invented to further develop printing have been the means of exploiting our timber limits as well as our pulp and paper industries, thus benefiting not only these large factories but all labouring classes of Canada. I wished to briefly point out these facts, although I am not prepared to discuss this resolution on its merits.

1012346,ca.proc.d.1934-02-05.18.1.12,1934-02-05,ed34bdbb-3fe8-4a8c-87a1-a2ad108b1e2b,ca.m.8281,Mr. J. H. STITT (Selkirk):,,UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF,REDUCTION OF HOURS OF LABOUR AND INCREASE OF PURCHASING POWER,,Before this motion is put to the house I should like to make a few extemporaneous remarks with regard to the proposal. I notice that the object of the resolution is to lessen the hours of labour and to increase the purchasing power of the masses of the Canadian people, and I am sure that every man in this house is sympathetic with that object.

I believe we have come in our history to a time when we must recognize that the era of the machine, as spoken of by the hon. member for East Hamilton (Mr. Mitchell) has given us in Canada and in the other industrial nations of the world a capacity to produce which means that our people are coming under the domination of the machine. In the first instance it was hoped that the machine would be the servant of man; he has now almost become its slave. I am not speaking in a way that is remarkable for one speaking from this side of the house. The other afternoon I heard a speech delivered by the right hon. gentleman who is now leader of the Senate, and referred to by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Maclnnis). He spoke about the concentration of power in a turbine, for instance, which is capable of performing the work of 9,000,000 men. He spoke also of the development of power in the Muscle Shoals project now under construction by the United States government, whereby power equal to the physical energy of 18,000,000 men will be produced. He also stated that the world has now on its hands a problem of
30,000,000 unemployed and the time is coming, nay, more, it is at hand when we cannot very much longer say to those people who are

out of work and who, in the words of the right hon. gentleman, are suffering degeneracy of character, that it will be sufficient if we give them the mere necessities of life. We have reached in our civilization a stage when the burning of coffee, the destruction of cotton, the cessation of the wheels of industry must be looked upon as mere palliatives. There must be more heroism in our plans and more radiical leadership. It is very hard, even in following the hon. gentlemen who have supported this resolution, to ascertain just how they are going to work out the proposals which they have made. It is very easy for any man in this house or in any other public assembly to speak for the mass of mankind, to be moved by heroic and humane impulses. It is another thing, however, to have humanity accept one's gospel or doctrine, and to work one's scheme according to the law and the conventions of the constitution under which man must work and really achieve practical results. I believe it was the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Hanbury) who spoke about the difficulties inherent in the constitution. Have we not reached the time when those difficulties will have to be overcome? After all, the constitution of Canada is only a law; it is only man-made and it can be changed. If the constitution stands in the way of orderly progress, the sooner that constitution is amended in a radical and progressive manner, the better.

But I should like to draw the attention of the house to something of a remarkable nature which has recently happened in the United States. Many constitutional lawyers wondered whether the program of President Roosevelt would be possible of realization under the strict constitution which they have in that country. It is common knowledge, no doubt, to every hon. member that in the United States constitution there is a clause which says that a contract is inviolable; that is, the inviolability of contract is protected by the supreme law of the United States. Yet just the other day in a judgment handed down by Chief Justice Hughes, who is one of the most outstanding jurists in that country, and who was, I believe, a presidential candidate on the Republican ticket, he makes in effect the following statement in regard to interference with contracts: ""In this national crisis, contracts must in some way be interfered with in order to make it possible for contracts to be performed at all."" That is the effect of his judgment.
There are many actions that could be taken. For instance, the other day, speaking without much preparation I stated that we are face to

Perhaps the minimum was so low, it was not effective, or perhaps it was not enforced; that might be the situation. At any rate, it was impossible for this industry in Winnipeg employing many operators, scientifically organized and not paying high wages, to supply in competition with Quebec firms any kind of reasonable product as required by the government.

I should like to make an observation which occurs to me, stimulated by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard in speaking about the limitations of the constitution. In this parliament we have extraordinary powers under the peace, order and good government clause of the constitution, and in Canada we have reached a crisis where, even if there is an increase in employment, there is not any appreciable decrease in the number of people who are going on relief. Might it not be said that the very fabric of the nation could be preserved only by having resort to that extraordinary power and that in this crisis we have more than ordinary powers to legislate concerning hours of labour, minimum wages and labour conditions than we would have ordinarily? I think an argument could be based on the peace, order and good government clause in the constitution to enable parliament now to go further than it could in 1929 or 1930.

There are some observations that I would like to make on the proposals put forward by the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps). He made the statement, I believe, that this government was wedded to a system.
I do not believe that this government is wedded to a system any more than are the hon. gentlemen in that corner of the house. But we are faced with a situation which exists.

I believe that the sweeping proposals enunciated in the speech from the throne, for instance that for the establishment of a central bank, are an actual facing of a situation which has been talked about for years [J. H. Stitt.]

and years, and are the best evidence that something is going to be done. The recent inquiry, moved by the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett), in regard to our internal trade, hours of labour and spread of prices between producer and consumer, is a most radical step. I feel that I can stand in this house to-day as a man who is supported by labour and by the farmers and fishermen of my riding, and say that I support a government that is more practical and more radical and that has more power and capacity to cope with the situation than any government that ever ruled in this country or any other body of men at the present time. When I made the statement last year that I was a Radical and at the same time a Conservative I meant what I said. And I believe there is evidence to prove that. I do not think that hon. gentlemen in the corner can expect very quickly to obtain a divorce from the present system. They will not get an interim judgment of judicial separation, or a divorce within three months to be made absolute within six months. I do not think they are accomplishing much by making the statement that this government is wedded to a system. Systems are not changed overnight. Systems were not created a priori; this system has grown. Liberals have contributed to this system, Liberals so-called have protected it, Socialists have declaimed against it, Conservatives have modified it, and Conservatives may change it. I have certain proposals to lay before this house with regard to increasing employment in this country, the reduction of interest rates, and embracing the marvellous opportunity which the government has to-day.

HUGH GUTHRIE (Minister of Justice) :,Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada,UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF,REDUCTION OF HOURS OF LABOUR AND INCREASE OF PURCHASING POWER,,Mr. Speaker, the object sought by the

mover of this resolution is very laudable, and his reasoning to the house in support of his motion was most praiseworthy. By this resolution the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps) simply desires to bring directly before the government what is alleged therein, namely that the government give immediate consideration to the problems there set out. The government can have no objection whatever to this motion passing, and at this moment I do not intend to deal at any great length with the subject. I wish to say definitely that for a long time this subject has engaged the best consideration that the government has been able to bestow upon it.

I am sorry that on the present occasion the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gordon), through indisposition, is not able to be present in the house and to take part in this debate, because of all the members of the government he is perhaps most familiar with the subject dealt with by this resolution.

The scope of discussion this afternoon has been somewhat broad. We have heard discussed such subjects as the machine age and interests rates, and a good deal of the discussion has had to do with what one might term the constitutional problems which confront the federal and the various provincial governments. In regard to the last point I can assure the house that it presents some very serious problems. The first object sought by the resolution is a reduction of the hours of labour, but when one discusses that question one is immediately confronted with what the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Hanbury) so well pointed out, namely that the provinces of this dominion cling very tenaciously to their provincial rights in regard to all questions pertaining to hours of labour, regulation of labour, wages and the like. While it is easy to suggest that a conference with the provinces should be called by the
Unemployment Relief-Mr. Guthrie

dominion, and that a broad discussion should take place with regard to certain constitutional amendments, it is a very difficult thing when these conferences do take place to secure that unanimity of opinion which in my humble judgment is necessary between the various provinces of Canada before any radical or serious amendment can be made to the Canadian constitution as laid down by the British North America Act. My experience, and I have had some in regard to interprovincial conferences has been that the dominion and the provinces have never yet been able to agree unanimously on a single important proposal laid before a conference for agreement. The nearest approach to agreement so far reached was at the recent conference held in the city of Ottawa. On that occasion the proposal did not relate to labour problems particularly. The proposal upon which we appeared likely to reach some agreement or some uniformity of opinion was in regard to the organization and incorporation of companies, the issue of prospectuses, the sale of companies' stocks, and the like. After many months of intensive labour a draft bill was prepared and submitted to the representatives of the nine provinces of Canada to ascertain if we could unite upon a uniform law in respect to such matters, a law which would prevail throughout the whole length and breadth of Canada. We do not yet know whether agreement will eventually be reached. The provincial representatives have taken the bill home with them, where they will consult their respective governments, and I believe a subsequent conference will be held about a month hence, the hope being that some agreement will be reached for a uniform law. However that is the first instance in my experience where an agreement sums likely to be reached in regard to constitutional difficulties or constitutional amendments.

I realize as fully as do other hon. members in the house that there are anomalies in the present constitution of the dominion. The difficulty is to apply suitable remedies by agreed amendments. I hope the time is not far distant when we may be able to arrange terms with the provinces in respect of some of the more pressing matters, one of which is assuredly the question of hours of labour throughout Canada which has been discussed this afternoon in respect of the present motion.
We in Canada enjoy many advantages under what we understand as a federal system of government. The United States, in like man-74726- 17

ner, has a federal system of government. There are many advantages under such a system, and the people of Canada enjoy those advantages, but there are also limitations. I refer particularly to the limitations under such a system imposed upon the federal government in respect of legislative authority. We became a party to the treaty of Versailles and to the labour clauses involved therein. In that treaty we agreed, as far as a federal government could agree, to certain clauses in regard to labour and hours of labour, but we insisted upon fhe inclusion of a special reservation applicable to the federal system pertaining in Canada-and to any other country which enjoys a federal system-whereby we might consult the various provinces and, if possible, persuade the provinces to legislate in regard to the treaty obligations which the federal government had undertaken. So far we have not succeeded in doing so. The question of hours of labour was discussed in one conference which I attended, not this year but previously, but no agreement was reached. All we have obtained so far is the promise from the various provinces that they will give serious consideration to the proposal. We have not yet reached an agreement. I realize that apart from the subject of education there is no question to which the provinces hold so tenaciously to their strict rights as they do in connection with questions involving property and civil rights, under which subject come all questions of contract, of wages and of hours of labour. Immediately you lay hands on the rights of the provinces in respect of these matters, difficulty arises.

I do not despair that at some time, perhaps in the near future, some satisfactory solution may be found between the provinces and the dominion in regard to hours of labour. I agree at once that in so far as federal employment or any employment at the instance of this government is concerned we can and do control hours of labour at the present time. In dominion contracts for public works and the like we have power to control the amount of wages paid to workmen, and if we so desire we can also control hours of labour. However, this applies only to what we may call dominion or federal works or contracts which comprise only a small percentage of the total work performed in Canada through private agencies. I doubt therefore if at the present time this parliament can legally do very much in the direction sought by the resolution before us.
It is true, as suggested by the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Stitt) that we might find a
Unemployment Relief-Mr. Guthrie

loop-hole in the general provision contained in the British North America Act which states that the federal parliament may pass legislation for peace, order and good government in Canada. We have already incorporated this provision in the federal statutes under the relief legislation of last session. However I doubt very much if at the present juncture we would be justified in treating the present situation as a calamity of such magnitude that the peace, order and good government of the country was actually threatened. There is an outstanding judgment of the judicial committee of the privy council in England which decides that grave emergencies may possibly arise when parliament would be entitled to take advantage of this particular clause in our constitution, notwithstanding all or any limitations which are otherwise imposed upon federal authority. But the instances cited in the judgment of possible emergencies are rebellion, invasion, plague, epidemics and the like. I doubt if any condition has so far arisen in Canada, serious as it has been in recent years which would justify this parliament in interfering with provincial rights by legislating in respect of the hours of labour in Canada under the peace, order and good government clause of the British North America Act.

The discussion this afternoon has been profitable and, in some respects, enlightening. Ail that is asked is that the government should give its serious and immediate consideration to two matters, the first being that of the reduction in the hours of labour and the second the increase of the purchasing power of the masses of the people in order that they may absorb all goods produced. I think I may state that these two matters are within the scope of the motion passed on Friday last by this house and that discussions in committee upon that reference will to a very large extent cover -the two matters now before us. A committee will be appointed within a day or two to consider the reference contained in the motion of Friday last. By the terms of that reference the committee is empowered to inquire particularly in regard to the ""labour conditions prevailing in industries supplying the requirements of such department and chain store organizations and the extent, if any, to which existing conditions have been brought about by the purchasing practices of such organizations, and the effect thereof upon the standard of living amongst those employed in such industries and organizations."" I fancy that under that this clause of the reference there will be a very full opportunity afforded the committee to cover
all the ground which would be covered by an investigation under the motion now before the house.

Meantime I can assure the hon. member for North Winnipeg that the government will give serious and immediate consideration to his proposal as set out in the present motion. At the same time I can assure him again that for many months the government have been giving consideration to this problem, and if we have not found a complete solution to it it is not because we have not endeavoured to do so. The government will accept this motion.

At that time the opposition wanted the government of that day to pass a measure bringing the eight hour day into effect in the steel industry in the province of Nova Scotia. Let me first read what the Minister of Trade and Commerce said, as reported at page 2371 of Hansard of May 21, 1930. Had he left it at that, and had the present Prime Minister not put his own interpretation upon what parliament might do, we might have let it go, but the present Prime Minister, speaking to the question of hours of labour in the steel industry, finished off his great oration and his argument by saying:

We have the opportunity and the jurisdiction; let us leave out all this talk about the province and assert that power affirmatively, and let it be understood in this country that when we agree to principles in treaties, in compacts and conventions, we mean what we say, and that our expressions are not mere sounding brass and tinkling cymbals.

not get the provinces to agree. He does not even tell us which province will not agree. Is it not time that the people of Canada should know what province is holding back progress? I think I can say without boasting, because the records speak for themselves, that the government of which I was a member did make some progress, although I will say that it did not progress fast enough. Up until 1930 when the present Prime Minister, the great constitutional lawyer of this country, showed me the way, I never had any doubt that the provinces had sole jurisdiction in this matter, but when the present Prime Minister, then leading the opposition, showed the way, the then Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) said: Then we will apply it not merely to one particular industry, but to them all. In that same year we passed an act known as 20-21 George V, an act respecting fair wages and an eight hour day for labour employed on public works of the Dominion of Canada. That act cut down the maximum hours of work on all public works to eight hours per day, whether it was public works undertaken by the government or by a contractor. Let me point out that the present government in its regulations pertaining to relief works did, in the first order in council it put through, provide this same principle, but in later years they reversed it, and in their agreements now with the provinces provision is made, not for a minimum wage, but a maximum wage-that they ought not to pay more than the government of Canada pays; and this is the first country in the whole civilized world in which a maximum rate of wages has been adopted instead of a minimum. Moved by Mr. Heenan, seconded by Mr. Beaubien:

WOODSWORTH (Winnipeg North Centre) moved:,,COOPERATIVE COMMONWEALTH,PRODUCTION AND DISTRIBUTION-PROPOSED ECONOMIC SYSTEM GIVING FIRST CONSIDERATION TO HUMAN NEEDS.,,Wffiereas, Canada still faces a serious economic situation, and
Whereas, the existing economic system is failing to function in the interests of the masses of the people, even denying to large numbers access to the means of livelihood;

Therefore be it resolved, that, in the opinion of this house, it is desirable that the present system should be superseded by one based on the principle of cooperative production and distribution in which human needs should be the first consideration.

He said: Mr. Speaker, two years ago, when I introduced a resolution on the cooperative commonwealth, the proposal may have seemed very academic. Last year I was able to announce the formation of a cooperative commonwealth federation and this year I am glad to be able to present a carefully considered program. This program, adopted at Regina last August, re-states and develops the point of view and the measures advanced for years in this house by the labour group and the United Farmers of Alberta group.

Frequently it has been said that labour men and farmers cannot work together. I know there are some superficial differences, but in the face of the great difficulties which exist at the present time many of these differences fade into insignificance. As a matter of fact in this house these two groups have found it possible to cooperate to an increasing degree year by year. Perhaps before going on to the program I might make a statement that will
Cooperative Commonwealth-Mr. Woodsworth

help clarify the situation in the minds of some of my fellow members. Our group is not strictly a party; it is rather a federation of provincial organizations. At present we have affiliated with the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation in Alberta the Canadian Labour party-Alberta

column1: Farmers of Alberta; in British Columbia the Associated C.C.F. clubs (B.C.) and the Socialist party of Canada, (B.C.); in Manitoba the Independent Labour party of Manitoba and Manitoba Farmer section of the C.C.F.; in New Brunswick the New Brunwick section of the C.C.F.; in Ontario the C.C.F. clubs of Ontario, the Labour conference of Ontario, and the LTnited Farmers of Ontario; in Quebec the C.C.F. clubs-the Quebec organization committee-and the Labour Partie du Canada; in Saskatchewan the Farmer-Labour group, and I may say that there are several other provincial groups whose applications have not been formally accepted as yet.

The resolution which I advance on behalf of our organization states that the capitalist system, as we now have it, has failed to function. I fancy a great many members will agree. Many however would say that this is merely a temporary defect in the system, and that one of these days we will come back. After an analysis of the general world situation and the history of the last one hundred years I cannot believe that this is possible. It is true that we may have some revival but I believe such revival must be very temporary in character. We believe that the only possible way of overcoming our difficulties is by the setting up of an economic system on an altogether different basis. But I can fancy a great many hon. members in the house tonight will ask, as they have asked before: ""But what other system is there, and how do you propose to establish it?"" Our manifesto gives the answer, and I beg the indulgence of the house to read the preamble to it, because it gives the general viewpoint that we are trying to advocate and makes intelligible a great many of our motions. I read:

The C.C.F. is a federation of organizations *whose purpose is the establishment in Canada of a cooperative commonwealth in which the principle regulating production, distribution and exchange will be the supplying of human needs and not the making of profits.

We aim to replace the present capitalist system, with its inherent injustice and inhumanity, by a social order from which the domination and exploitation of one class by another will be eliminated, in which economic planning will supersede unregulated private enterprise and competition, and in which genuine democratic self-government, based upon economic equality will be possible. The present order is marked by glaring inequalities of wealth and opportunity, by chaotic waste and

instability; and in an age of plenty it condemns the great mass of the people to poverty and insecurity. Power has become more and more concentrated into the hands of a small irresponsible minority of financiers and industrialists and to their predatory interests the majority are habitually sacrificed. When private profit is the main stimulus to economic effort, our society oscillates between periods of feverish prosperity in which the main benefits go to speculators and profiteers, and of catastrophic depression, in which the common man's normal state of insecurity and hardship is accenuated. We believe that these evils can be removed only in a planned and socialized economy in which our natural resources and the principal means of production and distribution are owned, controlled and operated by the people.

The new social order at which we aim is not one in which individuality will be crushed out by a system of regimentation. Nor shall we interfere with cultural rights of racial or religious minorities. What we seek is a proper collective organization of our economic resources such as will make possible a much greater degree of leisure and a much richer individual life for every citizen.

This social and economic transformation can be brought about by political action, through the election of a government inspired by the ideal of a cooperative commonwealth and supported by a majority of the people. We do not believe in change by violence. We consider that both the old parties in Canada are the instruments of capitalist interests and cannot serve as agent of social reconstruction, and that whatever the superficial differences between them, they are bound to carry on government in accordance with the dictates of the big business interests who finance them. The C.C.F. aims at political power in order to put an end to this capitalist domination of our political life. It is a democratic movement, a federation of farmer, labour and socialist organizations, financed by its own members and seeking to achieve its ends solely by constitutional methods. It appeals for support to all who believe that the time has come for a far-reaching reconstruction of our economic and political institutions and w'ho are willing to work together for the carrying out of the following policies.

May I pause for a moment to point out that this document answers a great many of the charges which have recently been made against the C.C.F. and its program. We do not believe in dictatorship; we believe in democracy. We would point out that to no small extent we have a financial dictatorship in Canada; we wish to have a democracy which will really represent the interests of the people. It has been stated very often when we have brought forward our proposals that they are identical with those of the Russians. I would say distinctly that we have no Russian affiliations whatever. Again and again we have stated that we have no connection whatever with the Communist party. Probably the body that has been working the nearest to the lines which we advocate is the British Labour party. We do use the term ""a planned
