column1: Cooperative Commonwealth-Mr. Woodsworth

and socialized economy,"" and therefore a great many people seek to put an end to us simply by calling us socialists. Well, everything depends upon the definition. Personally I have no objection whatever to the word ""socialism,"" but I would point out that socialism has a great many meanings to-day. In the co-operative commonwealth we have chosen a phrase into which we have the right to place whatever meaning we wish. I believe I could not do better than to repeat that which I said in my presidential address to the conference:

Socialism has so many variations that we hesitate to use the class name. Utopian socialism and Christian socialism, Marxian socialism and Fabianism, the Latin type, the German type, the Russian type-why not a Canadian type?

Perhaps it is because I am a Canadian of several generations, and have inherited the individualism common to all born on the American continent; yet with iiolitieal and social ideas profoundly influenced by British traditions and so-called Christian idealism; further with a rather wide and intimate knowledge of the various sections of the Canadian people-in any case, I am convinced that we may develop in Canada a distinctive type of socialism. I Befuse to follow slavishly the British model or the American model or the Russian model. We in Canada will solve our problems along our own lines. We have a goodly heritage, not only in natural resources but in pioneer traditions and social equipment. If we have the spirit of our fathers we can overcome the difficulties even of our complex modern world.

It has been charged again and again that we wanted to bring about changes by means of violence. At our conference we expressly and deliberately repudiated the charge, and said we wished to bring about changes in a peaceable and orderly fashion. The statement has often been made that the cooperative commonwealth which we advocate involves a highly centralized bureaucracy. There is nothing in our program to suggest that. We do believe that there are certain things which will have to be under the control of the federal government. There are other matters which will come under the control of the provincial governments and other matters which, as now, will come under the control of the municipal governments. We hope that there will be the possibility of a much wider degree of free cooperative effort than we have at the present time.

We start out to bring about these changes by the old and tried political method of electing a sufficient number of people to parliament so that there will be a majority in favour of the program we advocate. At the very outset of our program we place:
1.-Planning.

The establishment of a planned, socialized, economic order, in order to make possible the most efficient development of the national resources and the most equitable distribution of the national income.

To-day a great many people are convinced of the necessity for some form of planning. Even the Conservatives in Great Britain are beginning to talk planning. Mr. Roosevelt has made this idea almost a commonplace here on this continent. I noticed only within the last few days in a pamphlet published by the authority of the governments of the dominion and of the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, dealing with the world wheat problem and the London agreement, that these words are in the introduction:
The issue was clearly-Drift or Plan.
That certainly is coming to be the case. I quoted the other day a very striking passage from the speech of the Hon. Vincent Massey on the New Economic Nationalism, in which he said very clearly:
It must suffice for me to say that national planning will have to be the foundation of Canada's international relations.
I think we shall have to come to that. We point out in the explanatory note, one of which is attached to each plank in our platform, that-

The first step in this direction will be the setting up of a national planning commission, consisting of a small body of economists, engineers and statisticians assisted by an appropriate technical staff.

To-day there is no relationship between the giving of credit and the general national welfare. People have been going along in a happy-go-lucky sort of way. The old laissez-faire doctrine has predominated up to the present, and it has brought us almost to disaster.

Especially I would point out, as was done incidentally by one of my colleagues in the debate on the previous resolution, that to-day there is no proper equilibrium between the production of this country and the consuming power of the people. I am not going to-night into the knotty question as to whether this is purely a financial problem, as that may be touched upon by my hon. friend from Macleod (Mr. Coote) under another resolution. But whether it is purely a financial problem or whether it is not more fundamental and has to do with the ownership and control of the real wealth of this country, the fact is that we to-day are living in a age of abundance and yet a great number of our people are facing
Cooperative Commonwealth-Mr. Woodsworth
poverty and thousands are experiencing a great deal of anxiety.

I wish I had time to go into the concentration of industry which has taken place in Canada in recent years. I might refer to a very excellent article in a recent issue of the Canadian Forum dealing with Concentration in Canadian Industry. This article points out what we have tried to say again and again in this house in the last few years:
There were once more than forty banks in Canada. There are now ten. Of these the three largest have for some years done about seventy per cent of the business.

And so with trust companies. Four of the largest trust companies together have over seventy-seven per cent of the assets. And so with loan companies, three of which account for eighty-two per cent of the total assets.

It is the same with life insurance companies, * three of which control almost half of the total assets. The investment trust situation is very much the same. In our railway transportation we are facing to-day the prospect of amalgamation. Some of us remember that the fact was brought out years ago that Atlantic shipping is dominated by the North Atlantic Conference, of which the Canadian Pacific Railway Company is an important member. Five of the Canadian Pacific Railway directors are directors of Canadian Airways. And so . on. I shall not take time even to outline the article, but may I read a few words from its concluding paragraph? After referring to a few men of outstanding influence in this country it says:

Besides these titans there are some sixty others, including eleven directors of the Bank of Montreal and seven each of the Royal Bank and the Canadian Bank of Commerce-who, with a few powerful foreign interests, constitute the controlling group for Canadian finance, transportation, communications, powder, paper, electrical supplies, iron and steel, motor cars, agricultural implements, nickel, copper, chemicals, paints, cement, oil, rubber, textiles, milling, packing, tobacco, brewing, distilling, and motion pictures. Perhaps a hundred persons, here and abroad, decide what we shall eat, what we shall drink, wherewithal we shall be clothed, and most other of our activities.
One other very significant statement I quote:

At most only about 144.000 people in Canada receive income enough to be taxable; about 82.000 of these get $4,000 a year or less, and three per cent of the population gets twenty per cent of the income.

Surely that is sufficient evidence of the concentration of wealth in Canada, and the concentration of wealth has meant the concentration of power, and I think I am free to add that it has meant political power.
We say in our explanatory note:

The Cooperative Comomnwealth Federation will provide that in Canada the planning shall be done, not by a small group of capitalist magnates in their own interests, but by public servants acting in the public interest and responsible to the people as a whole.
We pass immediately from the idea of a plan to-

column2: -Socialization of Finance.

column1: Socialization of all financial machinerybanking, eurency, credit and insurance, to make possible the effective control of currency, credit and prices, and the supplying of new productive equipment for socially desirable purposes.
The control of finance is undoubtedly the first step in the control of our whole economy.
I noticed that not very long ago the press quoted Mr. Taschereau as having said:

In 1920 there were one hundred paper mills in Canada producing $100,000,000 a year in products, capitalized at $22,000,000, employing 31,000 employees and paying them $45,000,000 yearly. At the end of ten years there were 109 mills, producing $215,000,000 in products, but capitalized at $714,000,000. There had been an increase of 2,000 in employees but payrolls remained the same as in 1920. While product increased 115 per cent capitalization increased 3,500 per cent, roughly speaking.

Under those circumstances we feel that it is highly necessary that there should be a national investment board working in cooperation with a socialist banking system to mobilize and direct the unused surplus of production for socially desirable purposes. I can understand that a program of this kind would not go very far without the question of ownership being involved, and we pass to-

column2: -Social Ownership.

column1: Socialization (dominion, provincial or municipal) of transportation, communications, electric power and all other industries and' services essential to social planning and their operation under the general direction of the planning commission by competent managements freed from day to day political interference.

That, of course, visualizes the extension of our present form of administration by commissions, only we would insist that on these commissions the workers must be given a right to participate, and further that workers in public industries must be much more free to organize than they are at the present time.

We believe that only under a regime of public ownership and operation will the full benefits accruing from centralization of control and mass production be passed on to the consuming public. That I think is really where the difficulty will be found in controlling the mass buying that is taking place to-day by the big departmental stores, and which is shortly to come under review by the

column2: COMMONS

column1: Cooperative Commonwealth-Mr. Woodsworth

committee that is to be set up. I do not see how we are ultimately to pass on the economies of mass buying unless we have public ownership or effective control. Let me point out that, contrary to the charges made, the C.C.F. has never thought of socializing all industries. The charge is without foundation. Perhaps I had better read what we ourselves declare in the explanatory note:

Transportation, communications and electric power must come first in a list of industries to be socialized. Others, such as mining, pulp and paper and the distribution of milk, bread, coal and gasoline, in which exploitation, waste or financial malpractices are particularly prominent, must next be brought under social ownership and operation.

That is not so radical as some of our political opponents would have you believe. If the province of Quebec can as a province handle the distribution of liquor, I cannot for the life of me see why a province or municipality cannot handle the distribution of milk. If Ontario can handle the distribution of electrical power, through the hydro-electric system, I cannot see why a province or municipality cannot handle the distribution of coal. We have already proceeded a very considerable distance along the line of public control over these essential industries.

A great many people have told us that this means confiscation. That is a question which, at the Regina conference, we very carefully considered; and whilst we agree that it would be impossible beforehand to consider what should be done in each particular instance, we did lay down certain principles which we propose to follow. I will here read from the explanatory note, for I do not want any misunderstanding to exist on this very important point:

We do not propose any policy of outright confiscation. What we desire is the most stable and equitable transition to the cooperative commonwealth. It is impossible to decide the policies to be followed in particular cases in an uncertain future, but we insist upon certain broad principles. The welfare of the community must take supremacy over the claims of private wealth. In times of war human life has been conscripted. Should economic circumstances call for it, conscription of wealth would be more justifiable. We recognize the need for compensation in the case of individuals and institutions which must receive adequate maintenance during the transitional period before the planned economy becomes fully operative. But a C.C.F. government will not play the role of rescuing bankrupt private concerns for the benefit of promoters and stock and bondholders.

,Labour,,James Shaver Woodsworth,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=ee1cc492-9867-48d3-a612-c1fb491d2916&Language=E&Section=ALL

1012404,ca.proc.d.1934-02-05.19.1.3,1934-02-05,ee1cc492-9867-48d3-a612-c1fb491d2916,ca.m.1883,Mr. WOODSWORTH:,,COOPERATIVE COMMONWEALTH,PRODUCTION AND DISTRIBUTION-PROPOSED ECONOMIC SYSTEM GIVING FIRST CONSIDERATION TO HUMAN NEEDS.,,No, nor of enterprises which in the Prime Minister's own

We recognize that institutions and individuals are dependent upon certain investments, and the members in this corner of the house would be the last to see widows and orphans neglected. But we do not propose to allow men of great wealth to hide behind the widows and orphans. We want to see that security is given, not merely to the privileged few, but to all.
4.-Agriculture.

Security of tenure for the farmer upon his farm, on conditions to be laid down by individual provinces; insurance against unavoidable ciop failure; removal of the tariff burden from the operations of agriculture; encouragement of producers' and consumers' cooperatives; the restoration and maintenance of an equitable relationship between prices of agricultural products and those of other commodities and services; and improving the efficiency of export trade in farm products.

Again and again it has been stated by critics of the C.C.F. that we were going to take away the farms from the farmers. From the very first there has been nothing of that kind in our minds. We tried, in the very first conference we had a year ago, to guarantee the security of tenure to the farmer upon his farm. We recognize that the farmer is not an exploiter; rather, he is one of the worst exploited. To-day farming is still in the family farm stage, and as long as that is maintained there is no reason why under our scheme there should be any alteration in the ownership of farms.

I may say that in the province of Saskatchewan there are certain supporters of the C.C.F. who advocated that with respect to a limited number, farmers who were hopelessly mortgaged, their farms should be taken over by the state in order to save the owners from eviction.

1012406,ca.proc.d.1934-02-05.19.1.5,1934-02-05,ee1cc492-9867-48d3-a612-c1fb491d2916,ca.m.1883,Mr. WOODSWORTH:,,COOPERATIVE COMMONWEALTH,PRODUCTION AND DISTRIBUTION-PROPOSED ECONOMIC SYSTEM GIVING FIRST CONSIDERATION TO HUMAN NEEDS.,,There have been a good many different pamphlets. We advocate in that connection a great increase of purchasing power made possible by the social control of the financial system. Control must be directed towards increased employment, as laid down elsewhere, and towards the raising of prices of farm commodities by proper credit and foreign exchange policies, and by the extension of consumers' and producers' cooperatives.

column2: -External Trade.

column1: The regulation in accordance with the national plan of external trade through import and export boards.

We are firmly convinced that the old controversies between free traders and protectionists are now largely obsolete. In a world of nationally organized economies, Canada must organize the buying and selling of her main imports and exports under public boards, and take steps to regulate the flow of the less important commodities by a system of licensing. For that reason we would advocate the formation of a wheat board. That is in line with the developments we have in view. During the war we learned a good many things that should now in time of peace be carried into practice.

column2: -Cooperative Institutions.

column1: The encouragement by the public authority of both producers' and consumers' cooperative institutions.

The trouble to-day is that the small local cooperative institution is like a cake of ice in the gulf stream; it can exist only a short time: the influences opposed to it are too great. But under an arrangement such as we envisage, it would be possible for free cooperative institutions to flourish.

column2: -Labour Code.

column1: A national labour code to secure for the worker maximum income and leisure, insurance covering illness, accident, old age, and unemployment. freedom of association and effective participation in the management of his industry or profession.

I do not think it is necessary for me to go into details as to what would be involved in a labour code. I think we labour members in this corner, during the past thirteen years, have made it abundantly clear what we consider the minimum for the labouring people in this country. I would call attention however to one fact that always comes in to block us; it did so only a few minutes ago. I refer to the British North America Act. Now, we believe that it will be necessary to revise that act in order to make a proper labour code possible. We propose that the necessary amendments to the British North America Act shall

be obtained as speedily as required, safeguards being inserted to ensure that the existing rights of racial and religious minorities shall not be changed without the consent of those minorities. What we need chiefly to-day is to place in the hands of the national government more power to control national economic development. In Quebec there have been misrepresentations. I venture to say that no political party so far has so clearly safeguarded the rights of minorities as we have done in the section which I have read to the house.

column2: -Socialized Health Services.

column1: Publicly organized health, hospital and hospital medical services.

We believe that health services should be made at least as freely available as are educational services to-day. We are not concerned with whether the cost is borne by the dominion, the province or the municipality. We suggest that this is an enterprise in which dominion, provincial and municipal authorities, as well as the medical and dental professions, can cooperate.

column2: -British North America Act.

column1: The amendment of the Canadian constitution, without infringing upon racial or religious minority rights or upon legitimate provincial claims to autonomy, so as to give the Dominion government adequate powers to deal effectively with ui-gent economic problems which are essentially national in scope; the abolition of the Canadian senate.
As regards what we have in mind with respect to changes in the British North America Act, may I read this from the explanatory note:

The principle laid down in the Quebec resolutions of the fathers of confederation should be applied to the conditions of 1933, that ""there be a general government charged with matters of common interest to the whole country and local governments for each of the provinces charged with the control of local matters in their respective sections.""

So far as the Senate is concerned, I have not time to enter upon that, but we do not believe there is any place for a second chamber in a democracy such as we are supposed to have in Canada. Perhaps the least said at this time about the Senate, the better for the senators.

column2: -External Relations.

column1: A foreign policy designed to obtain international economic cooperation and to promote disarmament and world peace.

We stand resolutely against all participation in imperialist wars. And we do not believe in maintaining the empire as a means by which one group can exploit another. By all means let us stand together for sentimental and

column2: COMMONS

column1: Cooperative Commonwealth-Mr. Woodsworth
cultural purposes, but as H. N. Brailsford said not very long ago: ""Empire is debt."" That is shown in the case of Newfoundland; we do not propose to submit to that kind of thing.
Taxation and Public Finance.

A new taxation policy designed not only to raise public revenues but also to lessen the glaring inequalities of income and to provide funds for social services and the socialization of industry; the cessation of the debt creating system of public finance.
I think we in this corner have again and again explained what we mean by that, and perhaps under other resolutions during this session we shall have further opportunities of discussing the matter.

column2: -Freedom.

column1: Freedom of speech and assembly for all; repeal of section 98 of the criminal code; amendment of the Immigration Act to prevent the present inhuman policy of deportation; equal treatment before the law of all residents of Canada irrespective of race, nationality or religious or political beliefs.

I have on previous occasions expressed myself pretty fully with regard to section 98 of the criminal code and what is involved in it. I shall not enter upon that to-night, but shall simply quote again from the explanatory note:
We stand for full economic, political and religious liberty for all.

We have sometimes been accused by some of our opponents of being anti-religious, notwithstanding the fact that we have expressly stated that we want the fullest religious liberty for all and guarantee the minorities their full religious and cultural rights.
The next plank should perhaps be properly headed: "" Humanizing the law."" It reads:

column2: -Social Justice.

column1: The establishment of a commission composed of psychiatrists, psychologists, socially-minded jurists and social workers to deal with all matters pertaining to crime and punishment and the general administration of law, in order to humanize the law and to bring it into harmony with the needs of the people.
I hope at a later stage in this session the hon. member for Southeast Grey (Miss Mac-phail) will be here and able to -say a little more with regard to what this plank might involve.

column2: -An Emergency Program.

column1: The assumption by the Dominion government of direct responsibility for dealing with the present critical unemployment situation and for tendering suitable work or adequate maintenance; the adoption of measures to relieve the extremity of the crisis such as a program of
public spending on housing, and other enterprises that will increase the real wealth of Canada to be financed by the issue of credit based on the national wealth.
May I add a few words with regard to this:
Unemployed workers must be secured in the tenure of their homes, and the scale and methods of relief, at present altogether inadequate, must be such as to preserve decent human standards of living.
Perhaps, as I have only a few moments left, I might read another paragraph from our explanatory notes:

We propose to provide work and purchasing power for those now unemployed by a far-reaching program of public expenditure on housing, slum clearance, hospitals, libraries, schools, community halls, parks, recreational projects, reforestation, rural electrification, the elimination of grade crossings, and other similar projects in both town and country. This program, which would be financed by the issuance of credit based on the national wealth, would serve the double purpose of creating employment and meeting recognized social needs. Any steps which the government takes, under this emergency program, which may assist private business, must include guarantees of adequate wages and reasonable hours of work, and must be designed to further the advance towards the complete cooperative commonwealth.
We conclude the manifesto with this sentence:

No C.C.F. government will rest content until it has eradicated capitalism and put into operation the full program of socialized planning which will lead to the establishment in Canada of the cooperative commonwealth.

We have been told by some editorial writers that in Canada we already have altogether too much paternalism, but what of the way in which big business has drawn upon the resources of this country by way of charters, franchises, bonuses, tariffs and privileges of every description?-surely this is paternalism run wild. What we want to have in Canada is the planning and organizing of the productive and distributional agencies of the country in such a way as to provide for the needs of the Canadian people.
We very often have eulogies of capitalism. But what is the real situation to-day?

1012417,ca.proc.d.1934-02-05.19.1.16,1934-02-05,7ae29289-fb11-4e01-becc-dd3d1aa8a695,ca.m.8203,Mr. VALLANCE:,,COOPERATIVE COMMONWEALTH,PRODUCTION AND DISTRIBUTION-PROPOSED ECONOMIC SYSTEM GIVING FIRST CONSIDERATION TO HUMAN NEEDS.,,We have listened to

In the past year the people of Canada, ""untrained masses"" as they may be, by their ballots registered disapproval of anything the C.C.F. had to offer.

The handbook from which my hon. friend read is well worth reading. I believe even those of us who are most prejudiced against their policy will admit that in this book they have attempted to write something which would appeal to the electors. The convention was held in July. Since then three byelections have been held in Canada, one in New Brunswick, one in Quebec and one in the West. The ""untrained masses"" spoke, and there was not one C.C.F. victory. In British Columbia there was a provincial election and again the people spoke, but probably not as emphatically as they did in the rural centres. The C.C.F. realize, as I stated before, that without the huge rural vote they can never hope to sit to the right of the Speaker. In the last year their whole effort has been towards winning the confidence of the farmer and his support of their political viewpoint.

Last summer I did considerable travelling, and happened to be in Mackenzie constituency for a couple of weeks during the by-election. While in that constituency I met many people, and there was a disposition on the part of some to believe in the C.C.F. theories-and I use that word, because they are only theories. I see sitting in this chamber to-night others who were there at that time, and who were not supporting the candidate who won; I believe they will agree with me that as the day of the election approached we could see the C.C.F. fall as grain before the sickle. Had it not been for the storm on the Friday before the election, instead of John Angus MacMillan winning by 1,600 votes he would have won by 2,600. Throughout the campaign the C.C.F. attempted to tie the two old political parties together. It was suggested even that the Conservative candidate would be taken out and that we would bind our forces together. Nothing like that happened; we fought the Tory just as hard as we fought the C.C.F. and the United Front. It seemed to me a tragedy that two groups so closely related, the C.C.F. and the United Front, much more closely related than the Grits and the Tories, could not have united. There was only one reason they could not unite and that reason was Lewis St. George Stubbs. That was the reason they could not unite. I think they learned a lesson in that by-election. During the campaign we denounced the Tory policies and the record of the government. The Tory
Cooperative Commonwealth-Mr. MacNicol

party has a record and a history; we have a record and a policy. All the C.C.F. had to offer was a program, but the people chose to believe in some group that had accomplished something and had a hope for the future.

,Liberal,,John Vallance,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=7ae29289-fb11-4e01-becc-dd3d1aa8a695&Language=E&Section=ALL
1012445,ca.proc.d.1934-02-05.19.1.44,1934-02-05,4ec07e21-5e6c-41f8-9fa6-c6cbf37549e8,ca.m.3404,Mr. J. R. MacNIOOL (Toronto Northwest):,,COOPERATIVE COMMONWEALTH,PRODUCTION AND DISTRIBUTION-PROPOSED ECONOMIC SYSTEM GIVING FIRST CONSIDERATION TO HUMAN NEEDS.,,Mr. Speaker, the resolution on the order paper and now before the house has been very carefully worded. It reminds me of the old fable about the wolf in sheep's clothing: the ""wolf"" part appears about the middle of the resolution, and is contained in the words ""the principle of cooperative production and distribution,"" and the soft, gentle, ""sheep"" part is in the last few words, ""in which human needs should be the first consideration."" It is too cold now, the parks are filled with snow, and the soap boxes have been taken away but all summer long the people of Toronto and of other cities have had to listen to speeches on this same sort of resolution in various parks and from a hundred and one soap boxes and platforms throughout the city. As the speaker who has just sat down (Mr. Yallance) has intimated from soap boxes and platforms men of finance and men who have been successful in business and commerce have been denounced every night in the week. There has been never a good word said of those who have been successful in business and who have given employment in this country-only denunciation of all they are trying to do.

The question of profits has been mentioned. Production is to be without profits. Of course, no one in his right senses would produce without profit in any event, if he could help it; but the party in the southeast corner are expecting to produce without profits. A Cooperative Commonwealth Federation speaker,
S.
column2: W. Cheshie, speaking in Queen's Park, Toronto, on August 22, and reported in the Toronto Telegram of August 23, made an address advocating the C.C.F. doctrine, and then he advised his hearers to take the C.C.F. magazine, a weekly paper, and he made this statement:

column1: A profit of three cents per copy will therefore find its way to the coffers of the various clubs.
I might say that the paper sells for five cents a copy. I never heard of a manufacturer asking for a profit of 150 per cent on his product.
I have in my hand a letter from the Fuego Oil Company, dated October 1, 1930, from which I quote this sentence:

The usual profits from a guslier oil well are such that even the smallest stockholder can benefit remarkably. Remember also we have 10,600 acres of leases, and after one gusher blows in our leases and stock will rise to tremendous values.
Another letter was sent out on August 9, 1932, by the Fuego Oil Company. It says:

It holds untold promise for those of you who now take up the fight to make this field a truly successful oil field. It is already proven as a producing field, our well has opened up many miles of new potential production area, and with your help we will go on to make it pay you what you have expected from your investment.

I hope this oil company makes money. I hope that any company and any investor makes money. I hope that the directors of this oil company makes money. The directors are as follows: Agnes C. Macphail, M.P., Ceylon, Ontario; Margaret Macgregor, Toronto, Ontario; Mr. H. B. Miner, Milwaukee, Wisconsin; A. O. McArthur, Oyen, Alberta; Herbert J. Kelly, Toronto, Ontario. From this list of directors you will see, Mr. Speaker, that human frailty as evidenced in the desire to make profits is common to the whole human race, and everybody', when he or she gets the chance, likes to make an odd dollar or two honestly.

There is nothing new in this doctrine of cooperative production and distribution in which human need should be the first consideration. This doctrine was advocated in the time of Plato, which was long, long ago. It was advocated in the 18th century by Rousseau and Weishaupt, whose articles and speeches had much to do with causing the French revolution. It was advocated again in the 19th century by Karl Marx, who added to the theories of Rousseau and Weishaupt some of his own, together with those of Louis Engels. So there is nothing new in this at all, and it amazes me how men will get up on soap boxes in the parks and try to make their hearers believe that there is something new in this doctrine. Wherever it has been tried it has never gotten any'where, except in Russia at the present time, and certainly it will never get anywhere in a country like this.

I was very pleased with the very mild manner in which the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation spoke to-night. He was nothing like as strong in his language as I have heard him on other occasions, but that should not mislead anybody, he would not do that, but in all revolutions, once the revolution gets started, the mild-mannered leaders of the commencement are discarded and more vigorous leaders take charge and run the country through all the ramifications of a real revolution. That is what happened in France, where Mirabeau and Danton were sidetracked, and Robespierre came in. The same thing happened in Russia where Kerensky was sidetracked and the present group of rulers

column2: COMMONS

column1: Cooperative Commonwealth-Mr. MacNicol

inflicted the cooperative commonwealth policies on Russia, which were responsible for the slaughter of 500,000 Russians and destruction from one end of the country to the other, and for the annihilation of all forms of democratic and responsible government. It has been well said by the hon. member for South Battleford (Mr. Vallance) that there has not been any election in Russia since the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation of Russia took hold of the reins in that country.

I state, and I do not think it is necessary for me to bring quotations to my support, although I have ample quotations to prove it if I am challenged, that cooperative commonwealth federationism is socialism. There is no contradiction of that.

I go further and say that socialism and communism have identically the same objectives. There is no difference in their objectives. The final aim in each case is cooperative commonwealthism, and that is what is advocated for this country.

The speaker who sat down said something about violence, and I should like to quote something in that regard. I quite agree that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) does not by any means advocate a revolution, but I can hardly reconcile his mild manner to-night with the statement he made in parliament on February 1 of last year, when he said:

Let me say that we must distinguish clearly between the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation and communism. It i.s quite true that both believe in a changed social order, in a new economic system. The communists are convinced that this can be brought about only by violence.

That is right; that is the communist doctrine. The objective is the same in each case, but the communist says; We must reach our objective quickly by violence, while the socialist says: Let us have an educational campaign to try to attain our objective if we can by the vote. But the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation does not say how it would get its objective if it did not get it by the vote. But here is one clause in the cooperative commonwealth platform that was adopted at Regina, and if I am in error I hope that some member of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation will correct me. This plank reads:

The object of the confederation shall be to coordinate the activities of member organizations in order to promote through political action and other appropriate means, the establishment in Canada of a cooperative commonwealth in which the principle regulating production, distribution and exchange, will be the supplying of human needs and not the making of profits.
That little phrase in there, ""and other appropriate means"", is the joker as I see it.

,Conservative (1867-1942),,John Ritchie MacNicol,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=4ec07e21-5e6c-41f8-9fa6-c6cbf37549e8&Language=E&Section=ALL
1012446,ca.proc.d.1934-02-05.19.1.45,1934-02-05,intervention,,,,COOPERATIVE COMMONWEALTH,PRODUCTION AND DISTRIBUTION-PROPOSED ECONOMIC SYSTEM GIVING FIRST CONSIDERATION TO HUMAN NEEDS.,,Oh, oh.

,,,Some hon. MEMBERS:,
1012447,ca.proc.d.1934-02-05.19.1.46,1934-02-05,4ec07e21-5e6c-41f8-9fa6-c6cbf37549e8,ca.m.3404,Mr. MacNICOL:,,COOPERATIVE COMMONWEALTH,PRODUCTION AND DISTRIBUTION-PROPOSED ECONOMIC SYSTEM GIVING FIRST CONSIDERATION TO HUMAN NEEDS.,,It is all very well to laugh about it, but you will not likely get it by voting, so what are the appropriate means? The various speakers of the C.C.F. say that it must come and the leader of that party in his speech on February 1 last made this statement:

The communists are convinced that this can be brought about only by violence. They think it cannot be done in any other way. We believe that it may come in Canada by peaceful methods. . . . It may very well be that force may prove inevitable.

That corresponds to the joker. Now, the whole concentration of Marxism is contained in this resolution before us to-night. The resolution embodies the very first principle of the platform of Marx's doctrine, the principle of surplus value, which means that the profits of the factory do not belong to the capital invested in the factory, that the difference between what a factory sells its goods at and the cost at which they are manufactured belongs to the workers and none of it to the factory itself. Weill, no factory will remain in existence under such conditions.

Mark you, I am a firm believer in a fair return to labour. My whole life has been associated with labour-I am referring to the actual operatives, the men who work with their hands and heads and not so much with their tongues. I am referring to the man who produces in a factory and not the man who talks on a soap box; the man who does something with his hands or his head to develop the country, and not the man who tries to pull down the country. I repeat, I am in favour of labour getting a fair return, but I am satisfied that no industry in this country, no member of the C.C.F., would attempt to produce unless there was the possibility of a fair return. I think I am correct in that statement after having quoted what has been sent out by the concern to which I have referred, one of the directors of which is a leader in the C.C.F. This doctrine advocated in the resolution before us to-night has never been adopted in any country except as the result of class struggle in which the workers have massed together to overthrow the government of the country and thereby destroy not only the government but industry as well. I am opposed to class struggle. I am in favour of cooperation between the producer and the man who works in the factory to produce, and between them and the consumer. I cannot
Cooperative Commonwealth-Mr. MacNicol

, see how anyone of these three factors in the industrial system can be dissociated from the others. It seems to me their interests are identical, and if one fails all three parts of the industrial fabric of the country must also fail.

Now, the leader of the party, as he sat down, referred to the abundance under our system; the country, he said, has broken down while it has an abundance of everything. Arid of course, I inferred that could not possibly prevail, according to his argument, under a cooperative commonwealth. Well, there is a cooperative commonwealth in Russia and I look forward with great interest to what the hon. member for East Hamilton (Mr. Mitchell) will say in this regard when he gets up to speak, because I enjoyed reading what he said when he returned from Russia- not of course the trouble in Russia, nor the distress and suffering, because trouble and distress and suffering are to be deplored anywhere. I wish the Russian people every success, and I do not like to see trouble anywhere. The Russian people have behind them long years of success, but see what they have fallen to to-day under a cooperative commonwealth. As reported in the Toronto Daily Star on July 31, the hon. member for East Hamilton is reported as follows-and he will know whether he was correctly reported or not:

There are conditions in their factories which the Canadian people wouldn't stand for one minute. Girls walking around barefoot on iron filings, and that kind of thing. But worst of all, is the shortage of food. It's not too bad in Moscow, it's a little worse in Leningrad. But out in the country, it's terrible-especially in the south, where much of the food is grown. I saw I don't know how many hundreds of people starving, in Kharkov and Kiev.
The reporter asked him a question:

How did you know they were starving? ""I've got eyes. You don't need to be a scientist to know a person is starving. When whitefaced men and women, and children with distended bellies, crowd around the train at every station begging for money or food-then it's a pretty sure guess they're starving. I saw hundreds of them in Kharkov and Kiev. They didn't even have the traditional dried fish and cabbage soup. They were down to bread and water-and sometimes less than that. . . .
There may be a lot of nonsense talked about liberty-
Yes, Mr. Speaker; there has certainly been a good deal of such talk in this country and in this house-I am not referring to any particular comer of the house.
There may be a lot of nonsense talked about liberty; but you appreciate it after you have
been to Europe. Life is too short for that kind of thing. When I say this back home, some of them won't like it, but it's the truth; things are bad in Russia.

That is the effect which a cooperative commonwealth government has had on Russia, and no matter how bad conditions may be in Canada, I think it will be agreed that they are infinitely superior to anything in that country. I call to witness the hon. member for East Hamilton, who went over and made an investigation and was good enough to grant an interview to the press. I for one choose the Canadian system, and I am sure that that hon. gentleman will too, in preference to the Russian plan which the resolution calls for-* in my opinion straight communism as practised in Russia.

There was a Regina platform and a good deal has been said about it to-njght. I want to say a word or two in regard to it myself, not so much with respect to the planks particularly as in regard to what took place there. I agree with the leader of the C.C.F. that his desire is to keep communism out of his party, but he cannot keep communism out of it. The objective is communism or the result of communism, and this cropped up very vigorously at Regina. At the C.C.F. convention there was a delegate named William Moriarity, and I should like to quote what he said. A resolution had been moved to abolish violence from their platform. An amendment was moved by Mr. Moriarity, a delegate from Toronto seconded by Mr. E. K. Winch, delegate from Vancouver, and in the course of his remarks Mr. Moriarity said:

The methods suitable to capitalism are those of force,"" declared Moriarity. After citing examples where peaceful methods in Europe had failed, he declared, while he was in favour of constitutional methods: ""If the ruling class opposes the will of the people, we must use a method suitable to the occasion.""
Force is communism; force is what distinguishes communism from socialism, the objects of each being the same.

Mr. Moriarity attended the communistic convention at Moscow in March, 1925; in May, 1925, he attended the communistic convention at Glasgow, and in October, 1927, he was appointed organizer for the communist districts eight and nine, Alberta and British Columbia, with headquarters at Edmonton, Alberta. . At Regina there were other delegates who had communistic tendencies. I said once before and I will say again that if all those who have communistic tendencies are banished from the C.C.F. party, a large number will be put out of the party.

column2: COMMONS

column1: Cooperative Commonwealth-Mr. MacNicol

The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre stated that farming was not included in his program of socialization, but on February 1, 1933, he made this statement in giving a short definition of the cooperative commonwealth :

A community freed from the domination of irresponsible financial and economic power, in which all social means of production and distribution including land, are socially owned and controlled either by voluntarily organized groups of producers and consumers.
That includes land and land means farms.

,Conservative (1867-1942),,John Ritchie MacNicol,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=4ec07e21-5e6c-41f8-9fa6-c6cbf37549e8&Language=E&Section=ALL
1012448,ca.proc.d.1934-02-05.19.1.47,1934-02-05,ee1cc492-9867-48d3-a612-c1fb491d2916,ca.m.1883,Mr. WOODSWORTH:,,COOPERATIVE COMMONWEALTH,PRODUCTION AND DISTRIBUTION-PROPOSED ECONOMIC SYSTEM GIVING FIRST CONSIDERATION TO HUMAN NEEDS.,,Will the hon. gentleman permit me to say that if I recognize that, it was the statement as prepared two years ago by the United Farmers of Alberta.

,Labour,,James Shaver Woodsworth,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=ee1cc492-9867-48d3-a612-c1fb491d2916&Language=E&Section=ALL
1012449,ca.proc.d.1934-02-05.19.1.48,1934-02-05,4ec07e21-5e6c-41f8-9fa6-c6cbf37549e8,ca.m.3404,Mr. MacNICCML:,,COOPERATIVE COMMONWEALTH,PRODUCTION AND DISTRIBUTION-PROPOSED ECONOMIC SYSTEM GIVING FIRST CONSIDERATION TO HUMAN NEEDS.,,So that as the farmers are not in accord with socialization of land it was decided to delete that. I do not think the farmers will swallow that, hook, line and smker. The farmers in the old counties of Ontario who hewed their farms out of the forest, cultivated their land and handed it on to their families are not going to support any party which has even a back door design on their land.
I should like to quote what the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Maclnnis) said at Regina:
If the farmer wants a cooperative commonwealth in which everything is socialized but himself
Apparently there was a great deal of opposition at Regina to socializing land.
-then he had better have a cooperative commonwealth of his own.
If the farmer is to enjoy the benefits of cooperation, he will have to come half way.

There never was any half way in revolution; revolutions as a rule, once they got started, went all the way. If the farmer thinks he can afford to support the C.C.F. plan of socialization and will escape having his land socialized, then he is very much mistaken; it cannot be done.

The mover of the resolution spoke very strongly against the capitalistic system. Well, it is communism to denounce and advocate the overthrow of the capitalistic system. I should like to quote one of the clauses in the thesis of the Third Internationale at Moscow:

The communist international is the concentrated will of the world revolutionary proletariat; its mission is to organize the working class of the whole world for the overthrow of the capitalistic order and the establishment of communism.
So that the overthrow of the capitalistic system is the platform or plank of the Third Internationale communistic organization at
Moscow, and being a plank of the C.C.F. in Canada, that plank in any event is communistic.
I should like to say what the C.C.F. is proposing to do as announced on the soapboxes and platforms in Toronto during last summer, Mr. Philpott on May 27, made the statement:
The C.C.F. is adamant on one thing the whole banking system must be socialized.
And again, on June 3, he is reported as saying:

The C.C.F. was going to socialize all the essential tilings of society on a basis of service, not selfishness; on a basis of huma'n needs, not the satisfying of human greed. Among the essential things would be medical health service, milk, meat.

If the house will keep track of the number of things that are going to be socialized, it will observe there is hardly anything left. On June 10 Mr. Philpott is reported as stating that the capitalistic system must go. He goes on to say that it is: ""rotten,"" ""insane"" and ""dead."" I shall have a word to say about capitalism later on. Another C.C.F. speaker is quoted on July 16 as saying that the British North America Act, which is the basis of all our rights in this country must be abolished.

Then the hon. member for Southeast Grey is quoted on June 1 as stating that the insurance of Canada must be nationalized. Again Mr. Buckley, one of the C.C.F. leaders in Toronto, stated on August 29 that the Senate must be abolished. In Trinity park at Toronto, on August 30, C.C.F. speakers announced that when they obtained power there would be no salesmen. Of course salesmen would not be required under the system as announced tonight by the leader of the C.C.F., so that travellers and others engaged in selling throughout Canada would also be out of jobs.
Speaking at Stratford, on September 9, the hon. member for Southeast Grey is quoted as wishing to abolish all the businessmen in Canada, in a joking sense:

I believe that what makes the C.C.F. most appealing,"" said the speaker, ""is that it is so blatantly idealistic. We have had enough of the hard-headed business man and the superman. They should be dumped into the lake.""
Pretty hard treatment!

On November 18, Mr. Philpott, speaking in Massey hall, Toronto, announced that the public utilities, gasoline companies, milk, meat and coal companies will all be socialized and that the stock exchanges must be abolished. I wondered where all the money is to come from with which to do all this,
Cooperative Commonwealth-Mr. Luchkovich

because, as the leader of the opposition well said in speeches in many of the western provinces during the summer, confiscation without compensation would bring about civil war, or words to that effect. But the hon. member for Southeast Grey stated in a speech at Walkerton that a central bank would be established when they obtained power, with authority to print bills and lend same without interest. That kind of bank would be . as sound as the snowbanks out in front of this building.
Something was said by the mover of the resolution in reference to the concentration of wealth. I would like to give a few figures in that regard.
There are 80,568 depositors in Canada's eleven loan companies. The average deposit is S358.
There are 70,808 in Canada's thirteen trust companies. The average deposit is $384.
There are 2,821,876 credits to policy holders in Canada's twelve life insurance companies, the average deposit being $478.
There are 4,460,000 depositors in Canada's banks, the average deposit being $413.

I have not the figures of stock holdings in Canadian industrial companies, but I venture to say that in many they do not average any greater amounts than those I have just recounted. This all goes to show that the great masses of the investing Canadian people are investors in good securities, and the amount of their investments is far greater than the amount of the investments that we were led to believe earlier in the evening were held by the very rich.

Now I would like to say a word in reference to the capitalistic system. I am a believer in the capitalistic system, and I am opposed to the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation system. My observation of history is that the world owes more to the capitalistic system than it does to any other finance system under which man ever operated from the beginning of this world. The capitalistic system does give every man and woman an equal opportunity to strive, to study, to acquire knowledge, to achieve, to invest money in business, to give employment and to make what he can. It teaches them the laws of thrift; it teaches them that a man must live right to get along, and let his brother man do as he himself would like to do. I think it exemplifies the golden rule in its principles better than any other system. I am quite aware that there are and have been things going on that should be remedied, but these are violations of the capitalistic

system; they are not principles of the system, and members of this house, and those who sat here before us, have been trying through the years to improve these things. But the principles of the system itself in my humble opinion are the best that have been devised for the conduct of business in this world and for providing employment and giving people wide opportunity.

I have noted of late with much satisfaction that great labour unions in several cases have been dissociating themselves from the principles of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation. And well they should; there is little in common between true labourism and the principles of this federation. I worked for a quarter of a century with men associated with (he labour unions; I know what they have done and I am glad to give them credit for what they have done in alleviating conditions that men worked under a quarter or half a century ago. The labour unions have done a great deal of good in this country. They have had sane leaders who have cooperated with the governments of the day in trying to promote legislation beneficial to labour. I am in accord with any legislation that is good for labour. I worked with 900 men for many years. If in this house I can lift my voice in favour of raising the status of the average man who is called the workingman or labour man, I am going to do so.

I am glad to see that these organizations that have nothing in common with socialism or communism have dissociated themselves from the soap box oratory that has been flooding this country for the last two or three years, but which, thank goodness, is on the downgrade. It may have flourished a little for the last year or two, but to-day it is going downhill. Let me tell my good friend the hon. member for South Battleford that he need have no fear of the members in the southeast corner of this house or their party ever sitting to the right of the speaker as a government.

,Conservative (1867-1942),,John Ritchie MacNicol,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=4ec07e21-5e6c-41f8-9fa6-c6cbf37549e8&Language=E&Section=ALL
1012450,ca.proc.d.1934-02-05.19.1.49,1934-02-05,6d793e44-6c06-4c2c-9d9b-b6c100053abb,ca.m.6624,Mr. MICHAEL LUCHKOVICH (Vegre-ville):,,COOPERATIVE COMMONWEALTH,PRODUCTION AND DISTRIBUTION-PROPOSED ECONOMIC SYSTEM GIVING FIRST CONSIDERATION TO HUMAN NEEDS.,,Mr. Speaker, certain things that have emanated from at least two of the speakers to-night have brought me to my feet, and I intend to follow up the hon. member for South Battleford (Mr. Vallance), and the hon. member for Toronto Northwest (Mr. Mac-Nicol), who has just spoken.

I think it was the hon. member for Vancouver who interjected a remark during the speech made by the hon. member for South Battleford, that the members in this corner of the house do not agree. Well, I remember a speech that was made on the floor of this house last year by the very eloquent member for

column2: COMMONS

column1: Cooperative Commonwealth-Mr. Luchkovich

Vancouver, in which he twitted the member for Weyburn about his lack of knowledge of finance. The hon. member for Vancouver said: You know nothing about finance; you should stick to the tariff. There are others in the group also who hold that view with regard to these questions. Now I am not a communist; I agree with what the last speaker has said in regard to certain things that are taking place in the southern part of Russia especially in regard to agriculture. A little later I intend to say a few things about how agriculture is being carried on in Russia.

Speeches in . this house, not only on this subject but on other subjects, have disclosed three distinct orientations. Hon. members on the other side very frankly say they would conserve everything good we have in the system at the present time on the protective principle. Hon. members on this side would let things take their own course and, Micawber-like, wait for something to turn up; while the group in this corner would welcome planning on the cooperative principle. Whatever we may think about the policies of the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett), we at least must agree that he has very frankly advocated the policy of protection. He said he would raise the tariff, and he did so. On the other hand the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) as much as said, ""Put me in power and I will lower the tariff,"" As one speaker said in the west, the right hon. gentleman starts out by lowering the tariff and ends by raising it higher than it ever was during his regime. The other day I saw a cartoon in Maclean's magazine. The Prime Minister was pictured hunched on the back of a donkey, looking very dejected, and behind him were seen many unfulfilled promises. In an oval inset the leader of the opposition was sitting in a chair warming his feet at a fire.

,United Farmers of Alberta,,Michael Luchkovich,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=6d793e44-6c06-4c2c-9d9b-b6c100053abb&Language=E&Section=ALL
1012451,ca.proc.d.1934-02-05.19.1.50,1934-02-05,548a2ff3-1f52-4e62-ac08-965b22225e76,ca.m.2186,Mr. GOTT:,,COOPERATIVE COMMONWEALTH,PRODUCTION AND DISTRIBUTION-PROPOSED ECONOMIC SYSTEM GIVING FIRST CONSIDERATION TO HUMAN NEEDS.,,The last round-up.

,Conservative (1867-1942),,Eccles James Gott,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=548a2ff3-1f52-4e62-ac08-965b22225e76&Language=E&Section=ALL
1012452,ca.proc.d.1934-02-05.19.1.51,1934-02-05,6d793e44-6c06-4c2c-9d9b-b6c100053abb,ca.m.6624,Mr. LUCHKOVICH:,,COOPERATIVE COMMONWEALTH,PRODUCTION AND DISTRIBUTION-PROPOSED ECONOMIC SYSTEM GIVING FIRST CONSIDERATION TO HUMAN NEEDS.,,The Prime Minister was pictured as going to the last round-up, singing, ""Get along, little doggie, get along,"" but the leader of the opposition was pictured dozing near a fire, oblivious to the storm that was raging outside. I believe that no matter what we may say about the policy of the Prime Minister, to me and to hon. members even on this side of the house he looked more like Richard the Lion-Hearted on a very spirited prancer fighting what to many looked like a losing battle.
When I listened to the lengthy speech of the leader of the opposition I marvelled that a man could speak for four hours without uttering a single sentence in respect of the
[Mi. Luchkovich.]

policy through the instrumentality of which he was going to get this country out of the mess in which it now finds itself. There are people in Canada who still think that all we need is to change the government and put the other party in power, but during the next three, four or five years they will realize that the leader of the opposition cannot play the part of a magician and pidl out of a hat rabbits that are not there.

So, Mr. Speaker, the policy of one party in Canada is protection and the policy of the other party is low tariff. I have often heard members say in this house that all we need to do is lop away the mouldering branches. That argument is all right as far as it goes, but what are we to do if the whole tree is rotten? I suppose we will have to chop down the whole thing. Having this in view the resolution proposes that we set up in this country a cooperative commonwealth. So far as our friends to your left are concerned, Mr. Speaker, the only policy they have to offer is the old policy of the tariff. When Canada is ever brought down to an agricultural system administered as it now is in Russia I will no longer give my support to a cooperative movement. Of course I am going to be told that we cannot regiment people without destroying individual initiative and personal liberty. But I would like to ask this question: What does initiative mean in a world where it can no longer be exercised, a world where people are on the verge of starvation in the midst of plenty? There are hundreds of mechanics and technicians without work to do, through no fault of their own. They are just as able as other men who have been fortunate enough to secure positions. I deprecate the insinuation that the policy of nationalization and planning advocated by this group would inaugurate a system of communism such as is now being practised in Russia. I personally would not tolerate belonging to a group if I felt that its plan were to be modelled on the bolshevist prototype especially in regard to agriculture, and I submit my reason for that attitude.

For many months rumours of extreme hunger have been rife in regard to what formerly was the richest, the happiest and the most fertile part of Russia, namely the Ukraine. Letters have percolated into Canada.

I have read dozens of them, in which conditions in the southern part of Russia were painted. Many demonstrations have been held in New York, Boston and in other places on this continent against the hunger existing in the Ukraine. Hundreds of resolutions have been sent to the President of the United States and, I am sure, many have- been sent to the Prime Minister of Canada. Possibly the following resolution which was sent to the President of the United States will convey some idea of the conditions which now exist in the Ukraine:

Whereas, the population of the Ukraine, the richest and most fertile agricultural section of Russia, commonly known as "" the granary of Europe "" now part of the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics, is at the present moment in the throes of famine, many persons died and many are dying on account of the lack of food; and,

Whereas, the present condition of famine and starvation in the Ukraine has been brought about by systematic and ruthless collection of all grains and foodstuffs by the Russian Soviet government from the Ukrainian people and by using same for export and military purposes; and.
Whereas, the Russian Soviet government officially denies all reports of famine and starvation in the Ukraine, and denies to the civilized world the right to assist these starving people; and,
Whereas, Ukrainians in the United States are continuously receiving letters from their relatives in the Soviet Ukraine reporting deaths, disease, sickness and privation from lack of food; and,
Whereas, great newspapers of the world have substantiated these private reports in so far as their correspondents have been permitted to do so; and,
Whereas, requisitions of all grain in the Ukraine by the Soviet government is still going on, regardless of the fact that thousands are starving in this district for the want of food: and,
Whereas, in view of the above facts it appears that the Russian Soviet government is deliberately trying to wipe out the masses of the Ukrainian people.
Now therefore be it resolved:
I shall not read all that follows because it is too long. It gives the number of people at the meeting, and the place at which it was held, and concludes as follows:

We protest in strongest terms against the action of the soviet government in removing the grain and foodstuffs from the Ukrainian provinces so as to leave the inhabitants in such provinces in a starving and helpless condition, and we appeal to the public opinion o! the civilized world in the hope that they will protest and force the soviet government to cease this ruthless policy of starving the people oi the Ukraine.

I might be asked how I know all these things. I might be asked to substantiate the numbers who have died of hunger in Russia. It would be impossible for me to do so. All that I can say is that I have read dozens of letters coming to Canada from relatives in Russia, and some spoke of cannibalism and others of the population of whole villages
being decimated. I have some of these letters with me now but for lack of time I do not intend to read them.

Suffice it to say that agriculture is in a very bad way in Russia at the present time. In Europe Cardinal Innitzer of Vienna has sent out an appeal to the Roman Catholic world, especially in Europe, for help for these suffering millions. Appeals have also been sent from France and other countries in Europe. Mr. Mowinkel, the president of the league council, has tried to put this matter on the agenda of the League of Nations, but without success. There were too many axes to grind, too many impending non-aggression pacts, and so finally he handed the whole matter over to the International Red Cross. Dr. Am-mende, the secretary or president of the Minorities Association, also sent out an appeal to the civilized world. Even Leon Trotsky, the former leader of the bolshevik party, said in a recent article:
The agricultural policy in Russia is leading to bankruptcy.

Hon. gentlemen may ask what has all this to do with the resolution before us? I only bring the matter up because it has already been brought up on the floor of the house to-day. I bring it up because if any such thing should happen to agriculture in Canada I would be the first to dissociate myself from any form of cooperation that would result in anything happening in this country such as happened in Russia during the past year.

Walter Duranty, in a book called Tragedies of Russia, says that many former admirers of the policies in Russia who have been over there have now come back to this continent and in sullen silence have refused to answer any questions. Why? Because, as Duranty has said, no one who has not seen the reality would believe the report, and that the power of the dream will be greater than any truth.

The United Farmers of Alberta have always stood firm on the principle of equal rights for all and special privileges to none. It is my duty as a farmer member to sit in eternal vigilance in behalf of the farmer interests of the people who sent me here, and certainly any attempt to fetter the farmer such as is evidently taking place in Russia to-day would meet with my most vigorous condemnation and disapproval. No system of planning that would relegate farming to a position of inferiority should be tolerated. It would be hard to imagine the industrial east sending soldiers and tax collectors to the agricultural west as is now being done in Russia, and get away with it. Yet there are

column2: COMMONS

column1: Cooperative Commonwealth-Mr. Luchkovich

many in Canada to-day who say that an exorbitant toll is continually flowing from the prairies to St. James street. The economic structure of Canada is being destroyed at its mainspring notwithstanding what has been said in regard to Russia. So unbalanced and lopsided has it become that the outworn, rickety affair may topple over at any time, with the farmer, incidentally, at the bottom of the heap. And when a basic industry like agriculture fails it is bound to affect adversely all the other industries in Canada.

In my opinion no plan can succeed unless it accepts the principle of equalization of industrial opportunity as the guiding principle, and supplants the present pursuit of economic reward with the ideal of service as a motivating force; and no new social system can succeed unless the various elements are brought into systematic and harmonious working order for the common good. I believe that agriculture is in need of economic planning possibly more than any other industry. As a primary producer and ultimate consumer, the farmer gets hit both ways. Look at the great discrepancy between the price the farmer gets for his products and what he has to pay for other goods and services. Industrial equality and efficiency are thus essential to his best interests; and furthermore all inefficiency or waste that goes on in distribution reacts to his detriment, either as a producer or as a consumer.

I have spoken of cooperation as a third distinct orientation both in and outside of this house. As an essential working principle in helping the farmer to solve his difficulties it manifests itself in three ways-cooperative selling, cooperative buying and cooperative credit. Naturally the farmer must sell somewhat above the costs of production to make farming pay; since the price at which the farmer can afford to sell is determined by production costs, the intelligent buying of the goods and services that make up those costs is the second important problem; and the necessity for getting credit as cheaply as possible to facilitate selling and buying constitutes the third major factor.

The proper relation of prices will need special attention as it is not so much a problem of how much a farmer gets for his wheat as how much he can purchase when he gets it; that is, keeping the purchasing power of the agricultural dollar on a par with the dollar of other industries in order to bring about an equitable basis of exchange.
This, sir, is the problem of the farmer. It will require economic planning and radical monetary changes, and to this end it is
desirable that the present system should be superseded by one based on the principle of cooperative production and distribution in which human needs should be the first consideration.
